oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shabbos, the seventh, is the day on which all of creation completes its song, and that Jews sing along with Shabbos in their zemiros and at seudos made holy by the presence of the Avos and of Shabbos itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer: Hashem made seven days, seven lands and seven seas, and in each the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres. Music too has seven notes, and the Levi'im spent five years learning its wisdom. The Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the kinor, the harp, and is shaped like one; when the seven are complete the song begins. Through a story of the Stoliner patting the Blazhever Rav on the shoulder, he explains the passuk that the border 'touches the shoulder of Yam Kinneres'. Of all the Levi'im's daily psalms only Shabbos's is called 'a song', because Shabbos itself sings and Jews sing along with it. He speaks of the power of a niggun, of achdus in singing together, of preparing all week to feel Shabbos, of the holiness of Shabbos food, and of a Shabbos table where Shabbos itself is invited.

en: In each set of seven the seventh is the chosen one: Shabbos among days, Eretz Yisrael among lands, the Kinneres among seas.
The Kinneres is named for the kinor, a harp: once seven are complete, the song can begin.
Only the Levi'im's psalm for Shabbos opens with 'mizmor shir', because Shabbos itself sings, and Jews join its song.
The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes, and Shabbos is the day of achdus, so Jews singing together at the table and at shalosh seudos is a great pleasure to Hashem.
A person who did not prepare and guard himself during the week cannot feel the taste of Shabbos.
Shabbos food is holy, and a Shabbos meal must invite the 'King', Shabbos itself, through divrei Torah, zemiros and holy conversation instead of weekday talk.

title.en: The seventh sea: why the Kinneres sings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer on seven days, lands and seas, ties them to the seven notes of music that the Levi'im studied, and asks about the passuk on the border at Yam Kinneres. He explains that the Kinneres, the seventh sea, is named for the harp and shaped like one, and that Eretz Yisrael sings.

title.en: The Stoliner's pat on the shoulder

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Stoliner, after hearing the Blazhever Rav's holy kriyas haTorah, patted him on the shoulder so that he would daven Musaf. From this he explains the passuk: on Shabbos the border goes around Eretz Yisrael and pats the singing Kinneres on its shoulder.

title.en: Only Shabbos's psalm is a song

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the psalms the Levi'im sang each day and notes that only Shabbos's opens with 'Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos'. Shabbos itself sings, and since no person would dare sing to Hashem on his own, Jews sing along with Shabbos.

title.en: A day of song, and the power of a niggun

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Apter Rav that Shabbos is the time of singing, and a saying that one would sooner believe the seven seas dried up than that a Jew who can sing does not sing on Shabbos. He describes the singing of Friday night, the day meal and shalosh seudos, and explains that composing a true niggun takes a spirit close to ruach hakodesh.

title.en: Niggun as unity, Shabbos as achdus

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the niggunim of tzaddikim and of new composers sent down from Heaven, contrasting a real melody with a cat walking on a piano. The essence of a niggun is the unity of its notes; Shabbos is the secret of 'echad', so Jews singing zemiros together is a great pleasure to Hashem, and he laments those who leave before the zemiros.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and preparing for Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions Yedid Nefesh and calls shalosh seudos the peak of Shabbos's achdus, as in 'Atah echad'. He explains that one who did not guard himself in holiness during the week cannot feel Shabbos, urges preparing from motzaei Shabbos, and contrasts those who daven Shabbos with sweetness with those who talk during davening.

title.en: The Avos at the seudos; holy Shabbos food

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Avos come to the Shabbos seudos of Jews united in achdus, and that Shabbos food contains holiness. He tells how Reb Dovid'l Biderman of Yerushalayim ate a spoiled cholent in Meron, saying one may not disgrace Shabbos food.

title.en: Inviting the King to the Shabbos table

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the day itself is the oneg, and brings a mashal of a man who prepared a feast for the king but never invited him. So a lavish Shabbos meal without calling in Shabbos is lacking; the table should hold divrei Torah, zemiros and stories of tzaddikim, not business talk.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that just as the lowest soul, the month of Adar and the hidden story of the Megillah still hold Hashem's full presence, the light that descends through the four worlds remains bound to its Source.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's image of the soul descending like a seed from the father's brain to the toenails, which still carry its essence, and applies it, following the Sefer Yetzirah, to space, time and soul. In time, Nisan is the month of open miracles and Adar the last month, like our generation at the heels of Moshiach: a time of hester panim. Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak; Hashem is there but hidden. In the Megillah His name is absent and 'HaMelech' stands for Him, because Amalek conceals the Name, as shown by Rashi on 'kes Kah' and by gematria. The Megillah trains a person to see hidden miracles, even in the daily news, and to find Hashem's name between the lines. He then explains the four worlds of Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, and the Tanya's answer that even the lowest Jew remains bound to the Source.

en: The soul descends level by level like a seed that develops down to the toenails, yet the essence of the source remains even in the lowest part.
Following the Sefer Yetzirah, the same pattern appears in space, time and soul, with a Kodesh HaKodashim in each.
Adar, the last month, and our generation, the heels of Moshiach, are times of hester panim in which Hashem is present but unseen.
In the Megillah Hashem's name is hidden behind 'HaMelech' because Amalek conceals the Name and the Throne.
The Megillah is an exercise in reading between the lines to see hidden miracles and Hashem's hand in all events.
Hashem's light descended through the four worlds, Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, so that the creations could bear it.
Even the lowest Jew is truly a part of G-d above, bound to the Source and drawing his life through the tzaddikim of his generation.

Amalek and the incomplete Divine name

title.en: The soul's descent in space, time and soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews how the soul comes down like a seed developing from the head to the toenails, which still carry its essence. He brings the Sefer Yetzirah that space, time and soul mirror each other, and shows the Kodesh HaKodashim in each, meeting when the Kohen Gadol enters on Yom Kippur.

title.en: From Nisan to Adar, from Sinai to our generation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in time Nisan is the beginning, the month of open miracles, while Adar is the last month, like our generation at the heels of Moshiach. In both there is hester panim, Hashem's name is not seen, and what remains are questions on Hashem.

title.en: Adar as a cloak; the miracle of survival

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the questions after the Holocaust to the questions of the Jews in Haman's time, and explains that Adar comes from 'aderes', a cloak: Hashem is as present as in Nisan, only hidden. He says the very survival of Klal Yisrael among the nations, and its revival after the Holocaust, is the greatest miracle for one who opens his eyes.

title.en: HaMelech in the Megillah, and Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Megillah reads like a story without miracles or Hashem's name, yet 'HaMelech' refers to Hashem, who uses Achashverosh as His tool. He explains that the Name is hidden because of Amalek, bringing Rashi on 'kes Kah', and shows that HaMelech, Haman and 'kes Kah' each equal 95, while 'macho emcheh' equals the 107 of the completed Throne and Name.

title.en: Seeing the hidden hand: the medicine parable

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar's parable of a dying man for whom both the rare medicine and the one doctor who can give it arrive by ship within minutes, showing that perfect timing reveals Hashem's direction, as in the Megillah. He adds that rain, crops and the news are all miracles directed from Heaven, and that a person must train himself to see this hashgachah pratis.

title.en: Hashem's name between the lines of the Megillah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who sees the miracles can make the brachah on the Megillah, and that at every turning point Hashem's four-letter name appears in the initial or final letters of a phrase. He shows it in Haman's words 'zeh einenu shoveh li', with the letters reversed for strict judgment, and in Esther's 'yavo hamelech v'Haman hayom', in order for kindness.

title.en: From the Megillah back to the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that one who has learned to read the Megillah can see Hashem in the daily newspaper, and that with Moshiach the whole galus will be seen as one plan. He returns to the Tanya: the worst Jew is a part of G-d above just like the greatest tzaddik, only covered by sins, while tzaddikim are in contact with their soul and have ruach hakodesh.

title.en: The four worlds and the light of creation

summary.en: Reading 'v'kacha mamash' in the Tanya, the Mashgiach introduces the four worlds of the Kabbalah seforim. He explains that Hashem emanated a 'light', the least physical word available, and reduced it step by step into Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, down to our universe.

title.en: What the names of the worlds mean

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that because the world was created with loshon hakodesh, each Hebrew word describes its essence, as Adam HaRishon named the creatures. Atzilus comes from 'etzel', closest to Hashem; 'olam' from 'ne'elam', hidden; Beriah is creation from nothing; Yetzirah is forming. The light passed through these stages so that we can bear it, like viewing the sun through dark films.

title.en: The Tanya's answer: all are bound to the Source

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that the souls, down to the lowest, remain bound in a wondrous unity with the extension of Hashem's chochmah. This answers the question at the start of the perek about differing levels among Jews: like toenails, all share one essence that grew coarser, and the lowest Jew draws his life through the greatest tzaddik of the generation. He closes with the parable of electric current reduced through ever thinner wires.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach describes how people who strive higher keep Shabbos: guarding their speech, davening and learning at length, and reaching the peak of Shabbos at shalosh seudos with the zemer Bnei Heichala.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with speech on Shabbos: the kedushah of Shabbos limits a person's words to zemiros, brachos and Torah, and he should avoid talk that has no connection to Shabbos. He ties the three Shabbos meals to the Avos, with Friday night the meal of Yitzchak, and calls melave malka the meal of Dovid HaMelech. He discusses tefillas chatzos, a takanah and not an obligation, and tells of Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka. Since Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech too, while still making the Shabbos table pleasant for his family. He then speaks of the long Shabbos davening, Torah learned on Shabbos, Shabbos as a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel, and the great ratzon of Shabbos afternoon. He closes with shalosh seudos: little eating, the Arizal's zemer Bnei Heichala sung with dveikus, the angels who come to look, and the forces of evil that cannot enter.

en: The kedushah of Shabbos limits speech: words of zemiros, brachos and Torah, and not talk that has no connection to Shabbos.
The Friday night meal is the meal of Yitzchak, the three Shabbos meals correspond to the Avos, and melave malka is the meal of Dovid HaMelech.
Because Hashem created the world with speech and rested on Shabbos, a higher person keeps Shabbos with his speech as well.
The Shabbos davening is longer, with many mizmorim not said during the week, and Torah learned on Shabbos is far higher than Torah learned during the week.
The high point of Shabbos is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon and rachamim.
At shalosh seudos one eats very little; its essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala, sung together with dveikus.

Shabbos afternoon as a time of ratzon

title.en: Speech on Shabbos and the Shabbos meals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the kedushah of Shabbos limits speech to zemiros, brachos and words of holiness, and warns against talk unconnected to Shabbos. He ties the Friday night meal to Yitzchak, the three meals to the Avos, and melave malka to Dovid HaMelech.

title.en: Tefillas chatzos and Rebbe Elimelech's melave malka

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tefillas chatzos is a takanah and not an obligation, since a great level cannot be made a duty, and calls it the tefillah of Dovid. He then tells how Rebbe Elimelech kept melave malka with only tea and instructed his children about it.

title.en: Higher people keep Shabbos with their speech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that since the world was created with speech and Hashem rested on Shabbos, higher people refrain from idle words on Shabbos, yet must make a pleasant Shabbos table for their family. He brings the halachic side of not speaking about weekday work, the story of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's mother, and a reading of 'bechorish uvakatzir tishbos' as silence.

title.en: Tefillah and Torah on Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Divrei Emes that tefillah is the essence of Shabbos and describes the longer Shabbos davening with mizmorim not said during the week. He speaks of resting well so as to daven properly, of a fixed time for a chassidishe sefer, and of Torah learned on Shabbos being far higher than weekday Torah.

title.en: 'Between Me and Bnei Yisroel' and Shabbos afternoon

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Shabbos to the private talk of two close friends, a bond between Hashem and Klal Yisroel. For the choshuve Yidden Shabbos is a yichud with Hashem, and its high point is the afternoon, a time of great ratzon unlike weekday mincha; he speaks of eating shalosh seudos together with a minyan.

title.en: Shalosh seudos and the Arizal's zemiros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that at shalosh seudos one hardly eats and the essence is the zemiros, above all Bnei Heichala sung together with dveikus. He says the Arizal composed a zemer for each of the three meals, explains 'Bnei Heichala' as the King's palace children invited to eat with Him, and mentions the kabbalistic names of the meals, which he says he cannot explain.

title.en: Longing, angels and the closed door to evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the longing of shalosh seudos and how every small bite of the meal is precious. Angels come to see Jews sitting at shalosh seudos, the harsh judgments of weekday mincha are absent, and, as the zemer says, the brazen forces of evil cannot enter.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why shalosh seudos is the 'will of all wills', a time beyond time and without boundaries, and moves from there to Shabbos as a source of forgiveness and to the power of kiddush.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the three seudos of Shabbos and focuses on shalosh seudos. It is called raava d'raavin, the will of wills: all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha on comes a still greater et ratzon. A Jew should then awaken a strong desire to become upright, and even one who feels nothing gains by sitting with friends in love. Time and place are created things; before creation Hashem had a will to create, and shalosh seudos, before the first Sunday, stands above time. He demands seriousness at the table and tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov who once pushed a man for chatting then. Shalosh seudos, a boundless inheritance of Yaakov, extends past the end of Shabbos. He then speaks of Shabbos atoning for sin, the need to learn its halachos, the angels' blessing, teshuvah before kiddush, and the Satmar Rav's kiddush.

en: Shalosh seudos is called raava d'raavin because all of Shabbos is a time of favor, and from mincha a still greater et ratzon begins, a will within the will.
At shalosh seudos a Jew should arouse a great desire to become upright from now on, and if he cannot, he should at least want to have that desire.
Shalosh seudos stands above time: it corresponds to the moment before creation when Hashem willed to create the world, so it is a time to will to be created anew as an upright Jew.
Shalosh seudos is a boundless inheritance like Yaakov's, so its holiness continues for those still sitting at it after the time of Shabbos has passed.
Shabbos kept properly brings forgiveness of sins, but one cannot be a shomer Shabbos without learning the halachos of Shabbos.
Kiddush is testimony that Hashem created the world, so the Bnei Yissaschar says to do teshuvah before kiddush, and it must be said or heard with great kavanah.

candidateTopics: time and what stands above time

title.en: Shalosh seudos as raava d'raavin

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the three seudos correspond to the tefillos of Shabbos, says that shalosh seudos is a time for words of Torah and not idle talk, and explains why it is called the will of wills. He says a Jew should then resolve to become upright, or at least want to want it.

title.en: When one feels nothing: sitting with friends

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares a Shabbos without feeling to Avraham at the Akeidah, who saw the place from afar yet served with acceptance of the yoke. He explains that sitting at shalosh seudos with friends in love, like the angels who receive from one another, lets even one without enthusiasm absorb it, as standing near a tzaddik helps in davening.

title.en: Shalosh seudos is above time

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that time and place are created things, bringing the Gemara that the aron took up no space. Before creation there was no time, only Hashem's will to create; shalosh seudos, before the world's first day, is that time above time, so a Jew can then will to be created anew, and it is a great time for yeshuos, especially with a minyan.

title.en: Seriousness at shalosh seudos; the Rimanov story

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks that people sit seriously and not chat while waiting for shalosh seudos, using the minutes for Tehillim or a sefer. He tells of the Rebbe of Rimanov, who never bothered a Jew except once, when he pushed a man chatting at shalosh seudos, because it is a holy time.

title.en: Shalosh seudos extends Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the name 'shalosh seudos' means it includes all three meals, and that its et ratzon lasts past bentching and even past the time, so for those still sitting it is still Shabbos. This benefits souls released from Gehinnom on Shabbos; he notes two views in the seforim on how this works.

title.en: Torah after the time; Yaakov's boundless inheritance

summary.en: The Mashgiach says tzaddikim teach that divrei Torah at shalosh seudos should be said after the time, when the et ratzon is greater. He explains that Avraham and Yitzchak were promised Eretz Yisrael with borders, but Yaakov was promised that he would spread out in every direction, a nachalah without boundaries; shalosh seudos is Yaakov's inheritance, so the clock cannot end it.

title.en: Shabbos, forgiveness and teshuvah before kiddush

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that one who keeps Shabbos properly is forgiven even for idolatry, and stresses that being a shomer Shabbos requires learning its halachos, at least in Kitzur Shulchan Aruch before Mishnah Berurah. He brings the Gemara of the two angels who bless one who says Vayechulu, the dispute of the Maharal and the Taz whether teshuvah is needed, and the Bnei Yissaschar that one should do teshuvah before kiddush, since kiddush is testimony and a rasha cannot testify.

title.en: Kiddush with kavanah; the Satmar Rav's kiddush

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells children to say or follow kiddush in a siddur with great kavanah, and describes hearing the Satmar Rav's kiddush, when the whole beis medrash seemed to testify to creation, and the gathering of tzaddikim in Williamsburg after the war. He ends with a tzaddik who told people needing a yeshuah to come before kiddush, since one who says Vayechulu becomes a partner in creation, and closes the series on Shabbos.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the first parsha of tefillin speaks only of a 'remembrance' while the later ones speak of 'totafos', and shows how a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim in which the boy adds to the beauty of Hashem's own tefillin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by linking the bar mitzvah with tefillin, then notes that the parsha of Kadesh calls tefillin a 'remembrance between your eyes', while the other parshiyos say 'totafos'. He gives two answers. The first parsha speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn, so it is only a remembrance, as Chazal explain 'zichron teruah' of a Rosh Hashanah on Shabbos. And, from the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews had only the first two parshiyos, while 'totafos' means four. He explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, tells of Reb Dovid'l of Tolna leaving his boyhood games, and teaches that the boy must know his worth as Hashem's firstborn, add to the beauty of Hashem's tefillin, and search himself by the light of Torah as he enters his fourteenth year. He closes with a brachah.

en: The first parsha of tefillin calls them only a 'remembrance' because it speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn.
Following the Imrei Emes, in the desert the Jews wore tefillin with only the first two parshiyos, so the first parsha could not yet say 'totafos', which means four parshiyos.
Tefillin express a Jew's attachment to Hashem, and a bar mitzvah is a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim, leaving childish, yetzer-hara things for the service of Hashem.
A bar mitzvah boy must know how precious he is to Hashem, as Hashem's firstborn.
Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people, and the bar mitzvah boy must add to that beauty.
Entering his fourteenth year, the boy must search himself by the light of Torah for any 'chametz' that needs to be cleared out.

title.en: Why the first parsha says only 'remembrance'

summary.en: After an opening line linking the simcha of a bar mitzvah with tefillin, the Mashgiach asks why the parsha of Kadesh calls tefillin a 'remembrance' while the other parshiyos say 'totafos'. He answers that the first parsha speaks of Pesach, when tefillin are not worn, and then, from the Imrei Emes, that in the desert the Jews had only the first two parshiyos, while 'totafos' means four.

title.en: Bar mitzvah as a personal Yetzias Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tefillin as attachment to Hashem and the bar mitzvah as leaving childish things for the service of Hashem, tells how Reb Dovid'l of Tolna took leave of his boyhood play at his bar mitzvah, and from the parsha of Kadesh li chol bechor teaches that the boy must know he is precious to Hashem.

title.en: Adding to Hashem's tefillin; the fourteenth year

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's tefillin speak of the beauty of the Jewish people and that the boy must add to it, applies 'Or l'arba'ah asar bodkin es hachametz' to entering the fourteenth year, calls the first year after bar mitzvah the firstborn of a whole life, and closes with a brachah for the boy, his family and the final redemption.

oneLiner.en: On the opening of Tanya chapter three, the Mashgiach explains that the ten utterances of creation are the ten sefiros through which Hashem reveals Himself, and that a person carries them as intellect (Chabad) and seven character traits (Chagas Nehim).

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter three: each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros. He starts from the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation and the Gemara's question that only nine are found, and explains that these ten are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem appears to us, filtered down through the worlds like sunlight through darkened films. Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, though in him they are not called sefiros but Chabad (intellect) and seven midos. He defines chesed as giving and extending, gevurah as fear and withdrawal, tiferes as a new harmony, netzach and hod as two ways of survival, yesod as the power to create. He links the seven midos to music, the seven days of creation and Shabbos, contrasts Chabad's path of intellect with other Chassidim's path of emotion, and shows that the seven midos can serve good or evil, unlike the higher three.

en: The ten utterances of creation are ten powers, the sefiros, through which the infinite Hashem reveals Himself in creation in different aspects.
Man, created in the image of G-d, contains all ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; they are divided into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.
Chesed is extending oneself and giving; gevurah is fear and drawing into oneself; tiferes is the harmony that arises when the two meet.
Netzach and hod are two ways of survival, fighting the adversary or bending under pressure; yesod is the power to create.
Chabad, the intellect, is the father and root of the midos and is above this world, so in essence it has no evil, while the seven midos can be used for good or for evil.
Chesed and gevurah run through all of creation: male and female, summer and winter, the poles of a magnet, day and night.

title.en: Tanya chapter three and the ten utterances

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter three and recalls that nefesh, ruach and neshamah each consist of ten powers. He brings the Mishnah's ten utterances of creation, the Gemara's question that only nine are found and its answers, and explains that these ten are the sefiros through which the infinite Hashem appears in creation.

title.en: From the sefiros above to man below

summary.en: With the mashal of looking at the sun through darkened films, the Mashgiach describes how the light comes down from Atzilus to Asiyah. Man, in the image of G-d, contains the ten, but in him they are not called sefiros; the Mashgiach shows that Adam equals the filled-out Name of Havayah and divides the ten into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah: giving and withdrawing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chabad belongs only to man while midos are found even in animals. Chesed is love that extends itself and gives; gevurah is fear, a contraction into oneself. He applies this to the male as giver and the female as receiver, as seen in kiddushin and the kesubah.

title.en: Tiferes: a new harmony, not a mixture

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tiferes as the blending of chesed and gevurah, tied to the joining of mercy at the start of Bereishis and to the last utterance about a helpmate. With lemonade, a painting, a niggun and a second voice harmonizing, he shows that tiferes is a qualitatively new creation, and applies it to man and woman together.

title.en: Netzach, hod, yesod and the body

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines netzach as surviving by fighting and hod as surviving by yielding. He brings Pasach Eliyahu from the Tikkunei Zohar, which maps the sefiros onto the body: chesed the right arm, gevurah the left, tiferes the body, netzach and hod the two legs, yesod the organ of creation and malchus the mouth, and postpones explaining malchus.

title.en: Music, the days of creation and Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the seven sefiros to the seven notes of music, brings the harp of seven, eight and ten strings, and the Zohar's heichal opened only by song. Each day of creation was made with one sefira; when Shabbos completes the harp, one can sing zemiros, and the seven voices of the psalm said to welcome Shabbos correspond to the sefiros.

title.en: Chabad: the mochin and the Chabad derech

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that chochmah, binah and da'as are mochin, the father, mother and root of the midos. He explains the name Chabad Chassidus: serving Hashem through understanding creation, while most other Chassidim worked on love, fear and praise of Hashem and were wary of delving into what is above this world.

title.en: Animals have one trait, man has all

summary.en: Everything in creation comes from one or a combination of the ten. Each animal shows one sefira, like the lion, whose name equals gevurah, or the timid sheep, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed according to the Ramban, can be anything, with one or two sefiros dominant.

title.en: The seven midos for good and for evil

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the upper three are above this world and have no evil, while the seven lower midos, where the Tree of Knowledge took hold, can be good or bad. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on the passuk calling a forbidden union chesed, a judge who fears the powerful, and poetry that inflames the yetzer, and adds that the ten sons of Haman are the ten sefiros of impurity.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah in all creation; the Tanya's words

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows chesed and gevurah throughout creation: male and female, summer and winter, positive and negative charge, the poles of a magnet pointing north and south, day and night. He then reads the Tanya's words that each level contains ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros, divided into three mothers and seven doubles, and closes with intellect and midos in the human soul.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bris in the week of Parshas Ki Savo, the sixth week of consolation and the week of the middah of yesod, is a good sign, since the avodah of that week, like the bris, is to remove the orlah and reveal the good hidden in every Jew.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the verse calling the curses of Ki Savo 'the words of the covenant', and explains that the tochachah's harsh words are vessels of blessing that must be uncovered. That uncovering is bris milah: every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with the bris, is to remove the orlah covering it. Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, the week of yesod, the middah of the bris, and its avodah is to reveal that good. So too is Elul's avodah, hinted in the verse about the circumcision of the heart whose initials spell Elul. The haftorah's words about the nations he compares to milah and periah, and it ends with 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim'. A bris in this week is therefore a good sign, and he blesses the child, the family and Klal Yisrael.

en: The Mashgiach says the curses of Ki Savo, called 'the words of the covenant', are in truth vessels of blessing that need to be uncovered.
Every Jew has good in him, and his avodah, beginning with bris milah, is to remove the orlah that covers it.
Parshas Ki Savo is the sixth of the seven weeks of consolation, corresponding to the middah of bris, yesod, and its avodah is to reveal the good.
The avodah of Elul is the circumcision of the heart, as hinted in the verse whose initials spell Elul.
A bris in the sixth week, the week of 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim', is a good sign that the child will be a tzaddik.

title.en: The bris in the week of Ki Savo

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the curses of Ki Savo, called 'the words of the covenant', are hidden blessings, and that removing the orlah to reveal the good in every Jew is the matter of bris milah, of the sixth week of consolation (yesod) and of Elul. He compares the haftorah to milah and periah, calls a bris in this week a good sign, and closes with brachos.

catalogTitle: בר מצוה: bar mitzva Chaya Surah

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why Jewish kiddushin is learned from the purchase of Me'aras HaMachpelah: a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that outlives the body, and a bar mitzvah, when a boy receives his soul and the Torah as his kallah, is a wedding of the same kind.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Me'aras HaMachpelah, through which, the Midrashim say, Jewish prayers and souls pass. The Gemara learns that a woman is betrothed with money from Avraham's purchase of the cave from Efron. He asks why the happiest moment of life should be learned from a grave, and answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life: a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth and outlasts the body. He then brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, and the Torah, given as a kallah and an inheritance of all Jews, becomes his. Through the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah lives in every Jew. Finally he contrasts Efron's dust with the fire of zrizus the Torah needs, and blesses the boy, noting that the holy ancestors attend the simcha.

en: The Mashgiach says, citing the Midrashim, that Jewish prayers and souls pass through Me'aras HaMachpelah on their way up.
Kiddushin with money is learned from Avraham's purchase of the cave, because a Jewish marriage is a bond of souls that continues even after death.
A couple's souls were joined even before they were born, so every Jewish marriage is a union of souls.
A bar mitzvah is like a wedding: the boy receives his soul, which is Torah, and the Torah becomes betrothed to him as a kallah.
The Torah is the inheritance of every Jew and lies in his inner self even if he is not a talmid chacham.
Torah must be served with zrizus, the fire that rises, in contrast to the dust of Efron that brings sadness.

title.en: Kiddushin learned from the Machpelah

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Me'aras HaMachpelah as the gate of prayers and souls, notes that kiddushin with money is learned from its purchase, and asks why a wedding should be learned from a grave. He answers that Avraham wanted his bond with Sarah to continue beyond life, since a Jewish marriage is a union of souls that existed before birth.

title.en: The bar mitzvah as a wedding with the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah should be celebrated like a wedding, since the boy then receives his soul, which is Torah, and tells how Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai married off his son the night he turned thirteen. Through 'morasha kehillas Yaakov' and the Chasam Sofer on Haman he shows that the Torah is the inheritance and kallah of every Jew.

title.en: Efron's dust and the fire of zrizus

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the bar mitzvah to the parsha: Efron was a klipah in Chevron blocking the way to the Machpelah, and Avraham overcame it. Building on the father's words about the name Naftali Tzvi, he contrasts the fire of zrizus with the dust of Efron and sadness, then says the holy ancestors attend the simcha and blesses the boy.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Mashgiach explains that the curses of Parshas Ki Savo hold hidden blessings, just as the bris removes the orlah to reveal the inner holiness of a Jew, and that a father's bris is done purely for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the question of the Zera Kodesh: Parshas Bechukosai ends its curses with consolation, while Parshas Ki Savo ends with curses alone. He notes that at Har Gerizim and Har Eival only the curses are written, and the Gemara learns the blessings from them by a hekesh. He explains that great good is hidden in the Torah, covered by an orlah, and the bris reveals the inner point. Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem es levavcha', is the milah of the year, when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good; this is why Ki Savo is read then. The passuk itself answers: 'these are the words of the bris'. He links the bris to the completion of the child's formation and to Avraham Avinu, and contrasts it with Torah and chuppah, where other motives can enter. A bris is purely for Heaven, and he blesses the child accordingly.

en: Only the curses of Har Eival are written in Ki Savo; the blessings are learned from them by a hekesh, a sign that the blessings are contained within the curses.
Great good is hidden in the Torah under a covering like an orlah; when the orlah is removed, as at a bris, the inner point is revealed.
Elul, hinted in 'umal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha ve'es levav zarecha', is the bris milah of the year, when the hard months of Tamuz and Av are revealed as good.
The bris completes the formation of the child that began nine months earlier, just as Avraham Avinu with his bris was the completion of creation.
Unlike teaching Torah or arranging a chuppah, where other motives can enter, a father makes a bris purely for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Curses without consolation, and the hidden good

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zera Kodesh's wonder that Ki Savo, unlike Bechukosai, ends without consolation, and notes that only the curses are written while the Gemara learns the blessings from them. He explains that great good lies hidden under an orlah, and that the bris reveals Hashem's covenant with every Jew and the inner point that no place is empty of Him.

title.en: Blessings inside the curses; Elul as the bris of the year

summary.en: Using the hekesh and a rule of Tosafos in Zevachim, the Mashgiach shows that the blessings are contained in the curses. He then explains that Ki Savo is read in Elul because Elul is the milah of the year, hinted in 'umal Hashem', when Tamuz and Av are revealed as good, and compares this to the bris completing a child's formation.

title.en: 'These are the words of the bris' and Avraham Avinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers the opening question from the passuk 'eleh divrei habris': the curses are words of the bris, which reveals the inner point. He ties this to the end of the year, to the passuk 'umal Hashem' addressed to the generation of Moshiach and to 'levav zarecha', and to Avraham Avinu, whose holiness flares up at every bris and passes from father to child.

title.en: A bris purely for Heaven, and the blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's list of a father's duties to his son and contrasts Torah study and chuppah, where other motives can enter, as with Elisha ben Avuya's father, with the bris, which a father does with no motive but bringing his child into the covenant of Avraham. He closes with the blessing that just as the child entered the bris, so may he enter into Torah, chuppah and good deeds.

catalogTitle: ג' ראשונות' ז' תחתונות. העשר מכות נמשכים מהעשרה מאמרות' ונתגלה אח"כ בעשרת הדברות. (התחדשות של ניסן -קדושת המצות)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows how the Asarah Maamaros of creation were revealed through the Ten Makkos and given in the Aseres Hadibros, and how Nissan, the month of renewal and of emunah, and its matzah call on a person to renew himself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the three upper and seven lower levels, which become more tangible as they descend into the world. Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, but no one saw it; through the Ten Makkos He showed that every part of creation is His, against idolatry and against philosophers who say He left the world to run by itself. The makkos went in reverse order, from earthly to heavenly, and the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all. He turns to Nissan, the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and everything is renewed, and says a person should renew himself in avodas Hashem. Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah. Man contains all ten traits, so bread is his food; matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six. He urges care with good matzos, since Nissan's reishis of mercy shields from Tishrei's judgment.

en: Hashem created the world with the Asarah Maamaros, and through the Ten Makkos He showed openly that every sphere of creation is in His hand.
The makkos refuted both idolatry, with a separate god for each force, and the philosophers' view that Hashem no longer runs the world; He watches over every detail.
Nissan is the reishis of the year, when the world was actually created and Hashem's renewal filters down into nature, and a person should use it to renew himself in avodas Hashem.
Pesach is the time of emunah: Avraham, the first Jew, gave the mitzvah of emunah, and matzah is the food of emunah.
Matzah, three times forty-five, stands higher than bread, three times twenty-six, and a person should take care to have good matzos.

title.en: The Asarah Maamaros revealed in the Ten Makkos

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the three upper and seven lower levels, which grow more tangible as they descend and can be used for good or bad. He explains that through the Ten Makkos Hashem showed that He made the world with the Asarah Maamaros, against those who believe in a separate god for each force, and that the Torah, through the Aseres Hadibros, then contained it all.

title.en: Heavenly and earthly maamaros, makkos in reverse

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Bereishis is the first maamar and the source of the others, followed by three heavenly and then earthly maamaros. The makkos went in reverse order, from the earth up to the heavens, to show against the philosophers that Hashem controls every detail; he notes the sets of seven and three, and mentions that the seder plate and the makkos are also arranged by the ten sefiros.

title.en: Nissan, the reishis and month of renewal

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Nissan is the reishis: the world was conceived in Tishrei with judgment but actually created in Nissan with mercy, and the Jewish nation was formed then. Hashem's daily renewal of creation filters down in this month, and he describes how nature awakens in spring after the deadness of winter.

title.en: Renewing oneself in Nissan

summary.en: The Mashgiach says a person should use Nissan to renew himself in avodas Hashem, and tells of a tzaddik who found it hard to take time to answer a question because an hour in Nissan equals a whole day. He asks why a person should lag behind a renewed world, brings the Navi's image of the dry bones rising, and says the new clothes and cleaned house of Pesach should move a person to ask how he himself can become new.

title.en: Avraham, emunah and matzah

summary.en: The Mashgiach connects Nissan as reishis with Avraham Avinu, the first Jew, who gave the first mitzvah, emunah, which the Rambam counts first. Pesach is the time of emunah, and matzah, as the Zohar calls it, is the food of emunah; Avraham, the beginning, also ate matzah.

title.en: Animals, man and the food of man

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each animal was created with one trait, so its behavior can be predicted, while man, to whom every part of creation contributed, holds all ten and each person has his own dominant traits. Bread is therefore the food of man, and he brings the passuk that man lives not by bread alone but by what comes from the mouth of Hashem.

title.en: The Shem Havayah, Shabbos, and matzah above bread

summary.en: The Mashgiach divides the sefiros into Chabad, Chagas and Nehim, as seen in how tefillin straps are wound, and explains the Shem Havayah and its spelled-out form of ten letters. He connects reshus hayachid on Shabbos to Hashem, citing the Zohar, and shows that lechem is three times twenty-six while matzah is three times forty-five, so matzah is far higher.

title.en: Good matzos and the two reishis

summary.en: The Mashgiach urges care to have good, guarded matzos, since on Pesach a person charges himself with emunah for the year. He explains that there are two reishis, Nissan with mercy and Tishrei with judgment, and one who puts himself under Nissan's authority need not fear Rosh Hashanah. He closes with words on renewal.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the week of Toldos, the Mashgiach contrasts Yaakov's 'today' of Torah and mitzvos with Esav's 'today' of grabbing pleasure, describes the bar mitzvah as the boy's wedding with the Torah attended by his holy ancestors, and calls Toldos, the sixth sedra, a parsha of brachos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yaakov's words to Esav, 'sell me as of today your birthright', and describes two opposite ways of life. The upright Jew's 'today' is 'today to do them and tomorrow to receive their reward': Torah and good deeds now, reward later. The rasha's 'today' is 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die': grab the world now. Yaakov told Esav that their 'todays' differ, and Esav answered that he was going to die, so what was the birthright to him. Turning to the bar mitzvah, the Mashgiach says the boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos, and brings the Zohar that a bar mitzvah is celebrated like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah. His holy ancestors come to the simcha, so it must be taken seriously. He speaks of the gifts Hashem gives a bar mitzvah boy, notes that Toldos is a sedra of brachos, and blesses the boy.

en: The Mashgiach describes two opposite views of 'today': the upright Jew's, of doing mitzvos now and receiving reward later, and the rasha's, of grabbing pleasure now.
Yaakov's 'as of today' to Esav expresses that their two 'todays' are opposed.
At bar mitzvah a boy accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and becomes a chassan to the holy Torah, so the simcha is like a wedding.
The holy ancestors come to a child's simcha, so a bar mitzvah must be treated as a holy occasion, not merely a party.
Toldos is a sedra of brachos and the sixth sedra, which the Mashgiach associates with yesod, the foundation of bracha.

title.en: Two kinds of 'today'

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'sell me as of today your birthright' and contrasts the upright Jew's 'today to do them, tomorrow their reward' with the rasha's 'eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'. He then turns to the bar mitzvah boy, who accepts the yoke of Torah and mitzvos and should be a source of nachas.

title.en: A wedding with the Torah, attended by ancestors

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Zohar that a father must celebrate his son's bar mitzvah like a wedding, since the boy becomes a chassan to the Torah, and the holy sefarim that parents and grandparents come from Gan Eden to a child's simcha. Since the boy descends from great tzaddikim, the simcha is a holy occasion and not merely a party.

title.en: Gifts from Hashem and a sedra of brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of giving gifts at a bar mitzvah and says that above all Hashem should give the boy purity of soul and a desire for mitzvos. He notes that Toldos, the sixth sedra, is full of brachos, calls this a good sign, and blesses the boy to become a masmid and a gadol baTorah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in Elul, the Mashgiach ties the mitzvah of milah to the month through the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav", and closes with blessings for the child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk from parshas Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha v'es levav zar'echa", a passuk about milah of the heart, and connects it to the month of Elul; he speaks of a series of pesukim tied to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes the days of Elul, from Rosh Chodesh on, as a preparation for Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year. He returns to the passuk of milah and says this bris took place at an auspicious time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused. He ends with blessings that the child grow up to bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel and be dear before the Ribono shel Olam.

en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Nitzavim, "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha", in connection with the bris.
He speaks of a series of pesukim that are connected to Elul, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li".
The days of Elul lead up to Rosh Hashanah, the time that sets the whole year.
The bris took place at a good time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused.
He blesses the child to grow up and bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel.

title.en: The passuk of milah and the month of Elul

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk in Nitzavim "u'mal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha" and ties it to Elul, mentioning a series of pesukim connected to the month, among them "Ani l'dodi v'dodi li". He describes Elul as the lead-up to Rosh Hashanah, which sets the whole year.

title.en: A bris in the days of rachamim; blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the passuk of milah and says this bris came at an auspicious time, when the thirteen middos of rachamim are aroused. He blesses the child to grow up to bring nachas to his family and to Klal Yisroel.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Mashgiach explains through the Shem MiShmuel why "a new king arose over Egypt" when milah was neglected, and teaches that tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", bring the bar mitzvah and everyone present a daily renewal in avodas Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Shem MiShmuel, who brings a Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the Jews there not keeping milah, and asks what the connection is. He first brings the Avnei Nezer on a Midrash about Achashverosh's feast: when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, a gift from the Ribono shel Olam, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and that was the feast. The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when the Jews neglected it, Pharaoh seized the "chadash". So too a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which begin with "kadesh li kol bechor": a bechor means newness, and tefillin should renew a person's avodas Hashem every day. The Mashgiach contrasts weekday tefillin with Shabbos tefillin, explains that guests at a bar mitzvah gain renewal and so take back what the new king seized, and closes with blessings.

en: According to the Avnei Nezer, when the Jews did not keep Shabbos, the sitra achra seized its oneg, and this was Achashverosh's feast.
The Shem MiShmuel says milah brings chiyus and freshness; when it was neglected in Egypt, Pharaoh seized the newness, as "a new king arose".
Tefillin open with "kadesh li kol bechor", and bechor means something new; tefillin should give renewal in avodas Hashem every day.
Of all the mitzvos a bar mitzvah becomes obligated in, the main one is tefillin, and the seudah is on account of the tefillin.
Guests at a bar mitzvah recall their own bar mitzvah and gain renewal, taking back what the new king of Egypt seized.

title.en: Why "a new king" arose when milah was neglected

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shem MiShmuel's question on the Midrash linking "a new king arose over Egypt" to the neglect of milah. Through the Avnei Nezer on Achashverosh's feast he explains that a gift of Hashem left unused is seized by the sitra achra, and so Pharaoh seized the freshness that milah brings.

title.en: Tefillin and renewal at a bar mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a bar mitzvah receives tefillin, which open with "kadesh li kol bechor", a call to daily renewal in avodas Hashem. He contrasts weekday and Shabbos tefillin, says the guests too gain renewal and take back what the new king seized, and blesses the bar mitzvah and all present.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 3, the Mashgiach explains how Chochmah and Binah give birth to love and fear of Hashem, and how Da'as, deep and lasting concentration, makes those middos genuine and lasting.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the weeks of Sefirah, when the middos are refined, since good middos are the prerequisite for Torah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul has intellect (Chochmah, Binah, Da'as) and middos, and the intellect is the father and mother of the middos, with Da'as as the bridge that controls them; a bowl of cookies and a gifted child who is not yet responsible illustrate this. Chochmah is the flash of insight, Binah builds it up like bricks. Contemplating Hashem's greatness first produces yirah, a sense of shame before His greatness, and only afterwards true ahavah, the soul's thirst to cling to Hashem. A digression on Shechem and Dina explains the fiery words of love. Finally, Da'as means intense and lengthy concentration; without it love and fear are only empty imaginings. He ends with refining the middos through Sefirah.

en: Chochmah and Binah are the father and mother of the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites intellect with emotion and controls it.
Chochmah is a sudden flash of new insight whose origin a person does not know; Binah builds on it thought by thought until a complete structure stands.
Although ahavah ranks higher than yirah, in attaining them yirah must come first; genuine ahavah follows as a gift from Hashem.
True yirah is not fear of punishment but shame before Hashem's greatness, that so small a creature should go against His will.
Ahavah is the soul's yearning to cling to Hashem, like the fire in the heart that thirsts for the water of Chochmah.
Da'as is strong and lengthy concentration on Hashem's greatness; without it, love and fear are only imaginings.

title.en: Sefirah, middos and the text of chapter 3

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that middos are refined during Sefirah because they are the prerequisite for Torah, and links each chapter of Pirkei Avos to that week's middah. He then reads Tanya chapter 3: the soul is divided into intellect, Chochmah, Binah and Da'as, and middos, which are born of the intellect.

title.en: Da'as as the bridge: cookies and a katan

summary.en: Chochmah and Binah give birth to the middos, and Da'as is the bridge that unites them. With a jar of cookies the Mashgiach shows how understanding produces desire and how Da'as, responsibility, holds it in check; a child may be a genius but is not yet a bar da'as.

title.en: Chochmah as a flash, Binah as building

summary.en: Applied to avodas Hashem, seeing and contemplating Hashem's greatness gives birth to love or fear. The Mashgiach defines the intellect as the power in the mind that produces thought: Chochmah, koach mah, is a sudden flash of insight from Hashem, and Binah, from binyan, builds it brick by brick into a complete understanding.

title.en: Birchas Yotzer: fear, then love

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the birth of the middos in davening: in Birchas Yotzer one contemplates the greatness of creation and produces yirah, then in Ahavah Rabbah the great love of Hashem for Klal Yisroel arouses love in return, leading to the self-sacrifice of Krias Shema. This requires thinking deeply, not running through the words.

title.en: Why yirah must come before ahavah

summary.en: Though ahavah is the higher middah, genuine love can only come after fear. Fear is within a person's choice, love is not, as the spinach example shows; once a person has yirah, Hashem grants ahavah, the 'avodas matanah'. The Mashgiach brings the Maggid's words on the way of the 'ish' and a Gemara that yirah first is a good sign.

title.en: Higher fear is shame before greatness

summary.en: The Tanya begins with the higher fear of Hashem's greatness, not the lower fear of punishment. The Mashgiach compares it to everyone rising when a president enters, and brings the Gemara that yirah is busha, shame, and the reading of Bereishis as 'yarei boshes'. After the fear the heart flames with love.

title.en: The words of love by Shechem and Dina

summary.en: The four expressions of love in the Tanya appear in the parsha of Shechem and Dina. The Mashgiach explains that Shechem carried sparks of kedushah: he and Dina were reincarnated as Zimri and Kozbi and later as Rabbi Akiva and his wife, and their daughter became Osnas, Yosef's wife. The fierce words of love reflect those sparks struggling to break free of the klipah.

title.en: Love as the soul's thirst

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach says every Jew who unites his Chochmah and Binah can come to a burning love for Hashem, klos hanefesh, like a thirsty man in the desert who sees water. The fire in the heart thirsts for the water of Chochmah, the point of G-dliness in the soul; the other middos are branches of love and fear.

title.en: Da'as: intense and lasting focus

summary.en: Da'as, from 'yada', means connecting: to give birth one must fix the mind with strength and for a long time on Hashem's greatness, or the love and fear will be only empty imaginings. Da'as sustains the middos. The Mashgiach closes on purifying the middos during Sefirah, comparing the last weeks to refining silver to sterling.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, the Mashgiach explains that these days and the mitzvah of milah both lift a Jew above nature, drawing down the thirteen middos of rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah: their avodah is not according to nature, and a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun" to a place above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi, where Dovid HaMelech describes the order of nature: at night the animals rule, by day man goes out to his work. In these days a Jew rises at night, against that order. The ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, and the tenth, Yom Kippur, corresponds to "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", the maamar of eating, yet on that very day a Jew rises above nature. Above the sun there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches. According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation; milah too is above nature, and its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos. The child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a sign of yeshuos, and the Mashgiach closes with blessings.

en: The avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature: a Jew escapes from what is "under the sun".
Barchi Nafshi describes nature's order, in which man sleeps at night and works by day; in these days a Jew rises at night against that order.
Yom Kippur, the tenth day, corresponds to the tenth maamar, "lachem yihyeh l'ochlah", yet on it a Jew rises above the nature of eating.
Above nature there is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos that no sin reaches.
According to the Maharal, milah is on the eighth day because eight is above the seven days of creation, and milah is above nature.
The thirteen brisos of milah correspond to the thirteen middos and draw down rachamim upon Klal Yisroel.

naming a child after a tzaddik

title.en: Rising above nature in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the avodah of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah is above nature. He brings Barchi Nafshi's order of night and day, and explains that the ten days correspond to the ten maamaros, so that Yom Kippur matches the maamar of eating, yet on it a Jew rises above nature.

title.en: Milah above nature; blessings for the child

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that above the sun is complete rachamim, the thirteen middos. He brings the Maharal that milah, on the eighth day, is above nature, and says its thirteen brisos draw down the thirteen middos; the child, named after the Gerrer Rebbe, is a good sign for Klal Yisroel in these days. He closes by blessing the child to bring nachas to his parents, to Klal Yisroel and to the Ribono shel Olam, and wishes all a gmar chasimah tovah.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in Nissan, the Mashgiach explains that at Pesach daas went out of exile and the Jewish people 'became bar mitzvah', and that a boy becomes a baal daas both by reaching the full measure of daas and by accepting the yoke of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach praises the bar mitzvah boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile and at Pesach it went free, so the Jews came to daas and became, as it were, bar mitzvah. A boy once asked him why he felt no more daas than the day before; the Mashgiach answers that daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or a revi'is, and at thirteen the last drop completes it. This is why the Shabbos before Pesach is Shabbos HaGadol. A second way to become bar mitzvah is like a convert, by accepting the yoke of Heaven, which he ties to 'mishchu u'kchu lachem'. The boy became bar mitzvah on the day of the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together. He closes with the heavenly voice on a bar mitzvah, the gifts one may ask for, and brachos.

en: The Mashgiach brings from the seforim of the Arizal that in Mitzrayim daas was in exile, and at Pesach it went out, so the Jews came to daas.
Daas has a fixed measure like a kezayis or a revi'is; at thirteen the boy has its full measure, even if he cannot feel the last drop.
The Shabbos before Pesach is called Shabbos HaGadol because then the Jewish people became 'gedolim', no longer children.
There is a second way to become bar mitzvah, like a convert: by one's will, accepting the yoke of Heaven.
On the day of a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice tells the boy he is born today and may ask for gifts, and he asks for a heart to understand and to know Hashem.

candidateTopics: convert and acceptance of the yoke of Heaven

title.en: Daas goes out of exile; the measure of daas

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the boy's words on the korban Pesach and brings from the Arizal that at Pesach daas left its exile. He answers a bar mitzvah boy who felt no new daas: daas has a fixed measure, like a kezayis or revi'is, completed at thirteen.

title.en: Shabbos HaGadol, the convert, and Elyasaf ben De'uel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Shabbos HaGadol as the day the Jews became gedolim, and shows a second way of becoming bar mitzvah, like a convert who accepts the yoke of Heaven. He ties the boy's day to the nasi of Gad, Elyasaf ben De'uel, also called ben Reuel: daas and ratzon together.

title.en: Gifts from Heaven, the convert's Pesach, and brachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the custom of giving a bar mitzvah boy gifts: a heavenly voice tells him he is born today and may ask, and he asks for a heart to understand and to fear Hashem. He brings the Gemara on a convert and the korban Pesach, and closes with brachos for the boy and his family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Succos, the Mashgiach explains why the brachah is made over the lulav, which stands for Yosef the tzaddik, and sees in a bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin a sign for the child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the four species, which together hold all seven ushpizin: the three hadassim are Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, the two aravos Moshe and Aharon, the lulav Yosef and the esrog Dovid. The Gemara says the brachah is made over the lulav because it is the tallest. He brings the Chasam Sofer's question: the esrog stands for Dovid and malchus, which every brachah mentions, so why not make the brachah over it? The answer is that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia, who earned the name tzaddik through his test, and he reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' as Yosef defending his rank. Under one custom of the order of ushpizin, this day is Yosef's, and a bris, Yosef's mitzvah of guarding the covenant, on his day is no accident but a good sign for the child. He closes with brachos.

en: The four species correspond to the seven ushpizin: hadassim to the Avos, aravos to Moshe and Aharon, the lulav to Yosef and the esrog to Dovid.
The Chasam Sofer asks why the brachah is not made over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus, the theme of every brachah.
The brachah is made over the lulav because it is Yosef, the mashpia, the one who earned the name tzaddik.
In one order of the ushpizin, this day of Succos belongs to Yosef, and a bris on Yosef's day is by Divine providence, not chance.
The bris is the child's first kedushah and brings him into the level of Yosef the tzaddik, a good sign for his future.

title.en: Why the brachah is over the lulav

summary.en: The Mashgiach matches the four species to the seven ushpizin and brings the Chasam Sofer's question why the brachah is not over the esrog, which stands for Dovid and malchus. He answers that the lulav is Yosef, the mashpia and tzaddik, and reads 'there is none greater in this house than I' in this light.

title.en: A bris on Yosef's day of the ushpizin

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes two orders of the ushpizin, both true; by one custom this day is Yosef's, and a bris meal in the sukkah on Yosef's day, Yosef who excelled in guarding the covenant, is Divine providence and a sign for the child. He closes with brachos for the child and family.

catalogTitle: שלשה לבושים לנפש אלקות - מחשבה' דיבור' ד ומעשה. חב"ד- השגת התורה' אהבה' יראה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's teaching that the G-dly soul is clothed in the thought, speech and deed of the 613 mitzvos, with its intellect clothed in Torah study and its love and fear of Hashem as the roots of the positive and negative commandments.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns Tanya chapter four: besides its ten faculties, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed. Following the Arizal, every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in these three ways; they weave his garment in Gan Eden and correspond to his limbs, and a mitzvah never done is a missing limb, while Gehinnom only washes off sins. What cannot be done in deed must at least be learned and spoken about. Intellect is clothed in grasping the Pardes of Torah, each person according to the root of his soul, illustrated with the Vilna Gaon and with the Beis Yosef at the Arizal's shiurim. Love is the root of the positive commandments and fear of the negative ones, as the Ramban explains. The 248 mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King'; a human organ is truly an eye or a heart only when it serves Hashem, as the Midrash of the donkey without a heart shows. He closes by distinguishing fear of punishment from the higher fear of shame before Hashem's greatness.

en: Besides its ten faculties, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed, and every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in all three.
Mitzvos a person cannot do in deed he must at least learn and speak about; a mitzvah never fulfilled at all is a missing limb of the soul.
The intellect of the soul is clothed in grasping the Pardes of Torah, each person according to his ability and the root of his soul.
Love of Hashem is the root of the 248 positive commandments and fear of Hashem the root of the 365 prohibitions.
The 248 mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King', and a person's limbs are made to receive the corresponding heavenly powers.
True fear of Hashem is not fear of punishment but shame before His greatness.

title.en: Three garments of the G-dly soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter four: beyond the ten faculties learned before, the G-dly soul has three garments, thought, speech and deed. He brings the Arizal that every Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in all three, and explains that they form the garment of the soul in Gan Eden, the 'chaluka d'rabbanan' mentioned before putting on the tallis.

title.en: The barefoot father and the missing limb

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a great sage who appeared to his son in a dream in a wonderful garment but barefoot, because he had never collected tzedakah for the poor. He explains that the 613 mitzvos correspond to a person's limbs: Gehinnom only washes off the stain of a sin, but a mitzvah never done leaves a limb missing and requires coming back to the world.

title.en: Mitzvos one cannot perform

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what a person does with mitzvos he cannot perform, such as when his firstborn is a daughter or there is no Beis HaMikdash, and answers that he must at least think and speak about them by learning them; only one whom Heaven deems unable is excused. He then reads the Tanya's words on fulfilling the mitzvos in deed and studying their meaning and halachos in speech.

title.en: The orchard of Torah: Pardes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the intellect is clothed in grasping the 'Pardes' of Torah, its four layers of pshat, remez, drush and sod, likening it to a miner who digs beneath a beautiful field. He criticizes those who shy away from sod out of fear of greater responsibility, citing that one who keeps the first three and leaves out sod is called a 'pered', a mule.

title.en: Each according to the root of his soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that each person grasps Torah according to his capacity and the root of his soul, which can ascend through nefesh, ruach and neshamah, but some are rooted lower, like an inverted tree whose roots are in heaven. He illustrates with the Vilna Gaon, whom Reb Chaim of Volozhin could not equal, with the Beis Yosef who fell asleep at the Arizal's shiurim on sod, and adds that a person's intelligence also limits how far he can reach.

title.en: Love and fear as roots of the mitzvos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that the soul's Chabad is clothed in Torah study and its emotions, love and fear, in the mitzvos: love is the root of the positive commandments and fear of the prohibitions. He brings the Ramban on zachor and shamor and the Gemara's rule that a positive commandment overrides a prohibition, and explains that a mitzvah done without love, like tefillin put on by rote, withers like a cut flower, though every Jew has a hidden love.

title.en: The limbs of the King and the heartless donkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that the 248 positive mitzvos are the 'limbs of the King' and explains that Hashem, who has no body, emanates 248 powers that come down as human limbs. He then tells the Midrash of the lion who killed the donkey that demanded a toll, and the fox who ate its heart and claimed it never had one, ending with 'kaved lev Paroh'.

title.en: An eye that sees, a heart that fears

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'b'tzelem Elokim': each human organ is a receiver of a heavenly power, so the eye is called ayin because Hashem's 'seeing' is drawn into it, and a guarded eye becomes a chariot for that holiness; the heart corresponds to the heavenly heart of the thirty-two paths. An organ that does not serve Hashem, a heart without fear of Him or a knee that does not bow, is not truly that organ, which explains the Midrash about Pharaoh's heart.

title.en: Fear of punishment and fear of shame

summary.en: The Mashgiach distinguishes the lower fear of punishment, which is fear for oneself, from the true fear of shame before Hashem's greatness, illustrated by how no one would do something disgusting in front of a president. He brings the Gemara that 'His fear upon your faces' means shame, mentions Yechezkel's vision of the 'Adam' above and its counterpart in the Sitra Achra, and ends where the next passage begins.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the days of Sefirah, the Mashgiach explains why the heavenly call 'You are My son' comes in the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage': in a world casting off the yoke of Heaven, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with 'a time for every matter': each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him. In these days before Shavuos the Jews purify themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', newborn, and so too the bar mitzvah boy. He brings from the Zohar that at a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice says 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives new strengths and a yetzer tov; hence the custom of gifts, since He says 'ask of Me and I will give'. He then asks what this has to do with the psalm of 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal say speaks of the war of Gog and Magog, when the ropes of the yoke of Heaven are torn, as seen in the world today. He answers that once a boy grew up among emunah, but today being a son of Hashem is a great test, so he must, as 'I will tell of the decree' says, keep repeating 'You are My son'. He closes with brachos.

en: Each boy becomes bar mitzvah in a season suited to him; in the days before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves to stand before Hashem as a 'new offering', and so does the bar mitzvah boy.
At a bar mitzvah a heavenly voice proclaims 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and Hashem gives the boy new strengths and a yetzer tov.
The psalm of 'Why do the nations rage' speaks of the time before Moshiach when the yoke of Heaven is cast off, as is seen in the world today.
Once a boy grew up surrounded by emunah; today, exposed to heresy, immodesty and bad middos, being a son of Hashem is a great test.
Therefore, as 'I will tell of the decree' teaches, the boy must constantly repeat to himself that he is a child of Hashem and keep his bar mitzvah day fresh.

title.en: A new offering: the bar mitzvah as a rebirth

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties the bar mitzvah to its season: before Shavuos, Jews renew themselves as a 'new offering' to Hashem, and so does the boy. He brings from the Zohar that a heavenly voice calls 'You are My son, today I have begotten you', and explains the custom of bar mitzvah gifts by 'ask of Me and I will give'.

title.en: 'You are My son' in the psalm of Gog and Magog

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what the bar mitzvah has to do with the psalm 'Why do the nations rage', which Chazal apply to the war of Gog and Magog, when the yoke of Heaven is torn off, as he sees in the world today. He contrasts earlier generations, when a boy grew up surrounded by emunah, with today, when being a son of Hashem is a great test.

title.en: 'I will tell of the decree': repeating 'You are My son'

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'I will tell of the decree' as a law to repeat constantly that one is a child of Hashem and not act like those who go other ways. He tells the boy to keep his bar mitzvah day and its resolutions fresh, brings that the day should be celebrated like a wedding, and closes with brachos.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on Shemini Atzeres, the Mashgiach brings the Sefas Emes that 'give a portion to seven and also to eight' refers both to Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres and to milah on the eighth day, and sees in their meeting a sign for the child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash on the passuk 'give a portion to seven and also to eight': seven means the seven days of Sukkos, eight means Shemini Atzeres, and it also means milah on the eighth day. The Sefas Emes says both readings are one idea. The three parts of milah correspond to the three years of orlah, which must be removed so that the sign of the bris is revealed. Seven belongs to the world: the seventy bulls of Sukkos are brought for the nations, and seven is the days of creation. Eight, Shemini Atzeres and milah alike, is the private bond of the Jews with Hashem. Since nothing happens by chance, a bris on Shemini Atzeres is a good sign that this is a higher, Shemini Atzeres child. He blesses the family and Klal Yisroel, ties the eighth to the year of yovel, and prays for the geulah.

en: The Midrash reads 'seven and also eight' both as Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres and as milah on the eighth day, and the Sefas Emes says these are one idea.
The three stages of milah correspond to the three years of orlah, which must be removed before the sign of the bris is revealed.
Seven belongs to the world: the bulls of Sukkos are for the nations, while Shemini Atzeres has no connection with them.
Milah on the eighth day, like Shemini Atzeres, is the bond of union between the Jews and Hashem.
Because nothing happens by chance, a bris falling on Shemini Atzeres is a good sign that the child is of a higher kind.

title.en: Seven and eight: Shemini Atzeres and milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sefas Emes that 'a portion to seven and also to eight' means both Sukkos with Shemini Atzeres and the bris on the eighth day, explains eight as the private bond of the Jews with Hashem, and sees the bris on Shemini Atzeres as a sign for the child. He closes with blessings, a word on the yovel year, and a tefilah for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah in the week of Shelach, the Mashgiach explains that the celebration is public because the boy now joins the tzibbur, whose holiness comes from the good point in every Jew's heart, and that he becomes a shaliach of Hashem and of Klal Yisroel.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why a bar mitzvah is celebrated publicly. A chuppah joins families, and he heard from Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky that this is also why a kiddush is made for a newborn girl; but a bar mitzvah seems to be the boy's private bond with Hashem. He turns to the parsha: the Gemara learns that a davar shebikdusha needs ten from the 'eidah' of the meraglim, and Tosfos wonders why holiness is learned from the meraglim. The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a point in his heart no evil reaches; ten such points join into a holy whole, since combining exists only in good. A bar mitzvah boy can now complete a minyan, so his simcha belongs to the tzibbur. From Shelach he adds that every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem, and blesses the boy to be a faithful shaliach for Hashem and Klal Yisroel.

en: A chuppah, and a kiddush for a newborn girl, have a social side of joining families, but a bar mitzvah seems to be only the boy's own bond with Hashem.
The Gemara learns that a davar shebikdusha needs ten from the 'eidah' of the meraglim, and Tosfos wonders why holiness is derived from them.
Every Jew has a point in his heart that no evil reaches, and ten such points join together into a holy whole.
Joining together exists only in good, not in evil.
A bar mitzvah boy can now join a minyan and becomes part of the tzibbur, so his simcha is not a private matter.
Every Jew is sent into the world as a shaliach of Hashem and must be a faithful and successful one, like Kalev and Pinchas and unlike the meraglim.
