title.en: Why celebrate a bar mitzvah publicly?

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why a bar mitzvah, unlike a chuppah that joins families, is celebrated publicly, citing Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky on the kiddush for a newborn girl. He then brings the Gemara that learns the minyan for a davar shebikdusha from the meraglim, and Tosfos's wonder at this.

title.en: The point in every heart joins the tzibbur

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a point in his heart no evil reaches, and ten such points, even of people who are not tzaddikim, join into a holy whole, since combining exists only in good. A bar mitzvah boy can now complete a minyan, so the tzibbur gains a new power of good and the simcha is public.

title.en: Shelach: becoming a faithful shaliach

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that at bar mitzvah the boy becomes fit to be a shaliach, and from parshas Shelach contrasts the meraglim, who failed in their mission, with Kalev and Pinchas. Every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem, and he blesses the boy to fulfill his mission for Hashem and for Klal Yisroel and to bring nachas.

catalogTitle: קיום המצות במחשבה דיבור ומעשה. אע"פ שהתורה לבוש לנשמה היא יותר גדול ממנה. התורה נשתלשל למטה עד שיש באפשריות של המוח גשמי להשיג אלקות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the garments of Torah and mitzvos are greater than the soul they clothe, and how Hashem reduced His infinite will and wisdom into Torah so that a human mind can grasp it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's teaching that a Jew fulfils the mitzvos in thought, speech and action, and that these become garments for the soul. He shows how thought enters a mitzvah, especially where the Torah gives its reason, as with tzitzis, which include all 613 mitzvos, and sukkah. An ordinary garment is secondary to its wearer, yet here the garment is greater, because Torah is G-dliness itself. He qualifies this: the soul in the body is only its lowest part, as he explains through yibum and chalitzah, and at its root the Jewish soul is even above Torah. Since the Creator and His wisdom are one, the human mind cannot grasp Him; it is a different category, as one cannot hear a picture. Out of kindness Hashem reduced the Torah into concepts of this world, like water turned to ice, wrapped like radium in lead, and like Shlomo HaMelech's chain of meshalim.

en: Thought, speech and action in Torah and mitzvos are garments for the soul.
Unlike an ordinary garment, which is secondary to its wearer, the garment of Torah and mitzvos is greater than the soul, because Torah is G-dliness.
The part of the soul inside the body is only its lowest part; at its root the Jewish soul is above Torah.
The human mind was made to understand this world and cannot grasp Hashem, not for lack of intelligence but because G-dliness is outside its category.
Hashem reduced the Torah into concepts of this world, such as the laws of damages, so that our minds can grasp it.
Where one finds Hashem's greatness, that He cannot be grasped, one finds His humility, that He lowered His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos.

title.en: Three garments: thought, speech and action

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews that a Jew fulfils the mitzvos in thought, speech and action, which become garments for the soul, and notes that a suit is secondary to the person who wears it. He shows how learning Torah and putting on tefillin involve all three, and how, where the Torah gives a mitzvah's reason, that reason becomes part of the mitzvah.

title.en: Tzitzis, sukkah and the reason in mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tzitzis, which include all 613 mitzvos, differ from every other garment, and that the reason for sukkah is given in the Torah, so one keeps the reason in mind; where no reason is given, knowing one does a mitzvah is enough. He sums up thought, the brachah and the act, and asks how the garment can be greater than the soul.

title.en: Torah is G-dliness, so the garment is greater

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem and His wisdom are one, so Torah and every mitzvah are G-dliness itself, and the garment is more important than the soul. He notes that at its root the soul is higher than Torah, but sets that aside to speak of the soul as it is here.

title.en: The soul in the body and its root

summary.en: Through yibum and chalitzah the Mashgiach explains that the soul within the body is only its lowest part, like the foot inside a shoe, while the rest reaches heaven as an encompassing light. He then explains that Yisrael preceded the Torah in thought and the world was created for them, so at its root the soul is above Torah, and the Tanya speaks of the soul as it is in the body.

title.en: Hashem reduced Torah into worldly concepts

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that these garments are endlessly greater than the soul, and brings the Rambam that Hashem is the knower and the knowledge in one. Since our minds were made for this world, Hashem in great kindness reduced Torah into worldly cases such as an ox goring a cow.

title.en: Two meshalim: the picture and the water

summary.en: With a mashal he heard from his rebbe, seeing a symphony or hearing a picture, the Mashgiach shows that the mind cannot grasp G-dliness because it is the wrong faculty, not a weaker one. He then compares how steam becomes water and ice, the same substance in coarser forms, to how Hashem lowered the Torah into a form our minds can hold.

title.en: No probing His greatness

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem is called Ein Sof and that His greatness has no 'cheker', explaining the word as deep probing and philosophy, which cannot reach Him. He describes a person paying a high price for something a neighbor values at a quarter, and says the soul senses something special even when the mind does not.

title.en: His will and wisdom in the halachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that no thought can grasp Hashem's will and wisdom, which are the halachos of the Torah: that one who damages pays, and that one shelters in a sukkah though an architect would not advise it. He brings several pesukim and Chazal's teaching that where Hashem's greatness is found His humility is found, and reads the Tanya that Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos so the soul can grasp and fulfil them.

title.en: Radium in lead and Shlomo's meshalim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's greatness is that we cannot grasp Him and His humility is that He bent down to us, comparing Torah to radium carried safely in a lead container. He explains Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand meshalim as a chain, each explaining the one above it, as Hashem brought Torah down through the worlds to earth, so that people grasp it better than the angels.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Lech Lecha, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem promised Avraham the land only when he reached Shechem, the place of Yosef and of the bris, because Eretz Yisroel is earned through bris milah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that Hashem sent Avraham to a land without naming it, and even after he entered Eretz Yisroel did not reveal it to him; only when Avraham passed through to Shechem, Elon Moreh, did Hashem appear and say 'to your seed I will give this land', and Avraham built a mizbe'ach. The Mashgiach explains that bris milah belongs to Yosef, whose place is Shechem. The Jews merit Eretz Yisroel through bris and Torah, which is why the halacha requires mentioning bris and Torah in the blessing of the land. Parshas Lech Lecha is the parsha of bris milah, and Eretz Yisroel is the source of all good flowing to the world. He adds that Shechem is also where Yosef was taken and the first galus began, so the promise there assures the Jews will return. He blesses the family and prays for the geulah.

en: Hashem did not reveal to Avraham that this was the land until he reached Shechem, Elon Moreh, and only there promised it to his seed.
Bris milah belongs to Yosef, and Yosef's place is Shechem.
The Jews merit Eretz Yisroel through bris and Torah, which is why bris and Torah are mentioned in the blessing of the land.
Eretz Yisroel is the source from which all good influence flows to the whole world.
Shechem is also where Yosef was taken and the first galus began, so the promise given there assures the Jews of Eretz Yisroel.

candidateTopics: bris and Torah in the blessing of the land

title.en: Shechem, the bris and Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Hashem promised Avraham the land only at Shechem, and answers that Shechem is Yosef's place, the place of the bris, through which the Jews merit Eretz Yisroel, as the blessing of the land shows. He adds that Shechem is where the first galus began, and closes with blessings for the family and for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bar mitzvah, the Mashgiach explains that the bar mitzvah day is a 'wedding day' on which the boy is crowned with a new, higher soul, and that at thirteen it becomes visible which family and tree he comes from.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, at his son's bar mitzvah, expounded the passuk 'Go out and see, daughters of Zion' as referring to the crown the Shechinah gives the bar mitzvah boy, calling the day his wedding day. From this the obligation to make a bar mitzvah celebration entered the Shulchan Aruch and the Magen Avraham. The bride, he explains, is the neshamah yeseirah, a new and higher soul, received like the Shabbos soul as a crown. He then asks why bar mitzvah is at thirteen and why it is learned from Shimon and Levi, 'brothers of Dinah': at thirteen a boy's true nature and family surface, as a leaf shows its tree. Finally he brings the heavenly voice declaring 'You are My son', explains the custom of bar mitzvah gifts as a reflection of heavenly gifts, and addresses the boy about his first tefillin and the value of youth.

en: According to the Midrash the Mashgiach cites, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai read 'on the day of his wedding and the day of his heart's joy' as the bar mitzvah day, when the Shechinah crowns the boy.
The bride of the bar mitzvah 'wedding' is the neshamah yeseirah, a new and higher soul that gives the boy a drive to serve Hashem, received as a crown like the extra soul of Shabbos.
Bar mitzvah at thirteen is learned from Levi being called 'ish' at that age, in the passuk about Shimon and Levi, the brothers of Dinah.
At thirteen a boy's true character and the family he belongs to come to the surface, as Shimon and Levi showed when they stood up for their sister.
Bar mitzvah gifts given below reflect the gifts showered on the boy from Heaven, above all a new and higher soul.

candidateTopics: bar mitzvah as a wedding day

title.en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's bar mitzvah and the crown of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai at his son's bar mitzvah, reading 'Go out and see, daughters of Zion' as the crown the Shechinah gives the boy on his 'wedding day', and notes that the obligation to celebrate entered the Shulchan Aruch. He explains that the bride is the neshamah yeseirah, received like the Shabbos soul as a crown.

title.en: Why thirteen: Shimon and Levi, brothers of Dinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why bar mitzvah is at thirteen and brings the derivation from Levi being called 'ish' in the passuk of Shimon and Levi. He explains, through 'the lads grew up' and the image of a leaf that shows its tree, that at thirteen a boy's true nature and family come out, as Shimon and Levi showed by standing up for their sister.

title.en: The heavenly voice, the gifts, and words to the boy

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the teaching that on the bar mitzvah day a heavenly voice tells the boy 'You are My son', and asks why a bar mitzvah boy receives gifts like a chosson and kallah; he answers that what is done below reflects the heavenly gifts, above all a new soul. He then addresses the boy about his first tefillin and Elokai Neshama, and tells him that greatness is built by working in the young years.

oneLiner.en: At a bris, the Mashgiach explains that Hashem comes to every bris twice: on the day of the milah, when He holds the mohel's hand and Himself signs the bris, and on the third day, to visit and bless.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Rashi on 'Vayeira': on the third day after Avraham's milah, Hashem came to ask after his welfare. Since everything stated about milah is eternal, the same happens at every bris, and Hashem comes twice. The first time is at the bris itself. On the verse 'v'charos imo habris' he explains that Avraham feared he might not perform the milah properly, so Hashem held his hand; so too at every bris Hashem holds the mohel's hand like a scribe holds his pen. A signature must come from its owner, and citing the Zera Kodesh he says Hashem's name is inscribed through the bris, so Hashem Himself signs, as the blessing says 'chasam b'os bris kodesh'. The second time is on the third day. He adds that at a bris everyone present has a share, ties Parshas Chayei Sarah's purchase of Chevron to the place of Avraham's bris, and closes with blessings for the child and family.

en: Because what is said about milah is eternal, Hashem's visit to Avraham on the third day after his milah repeats at every bris.
Hashem comes to a bris twice: at the bris itself and on the third day.
Just as Hashem held Avraham's hand at his bris, He holds the mohel's hand at every bris.
The blessing 'chasam b'os bris kodesh' means Hashem Himself signs the bris, since a signature must come from its owner.
At a bris everyone present has a share, unlike other simchos where only some are honored.

title.en: Hashem comes to every bris twice

summary.en: The Mashgiach starts from Rashi that Hashem visited Avraham on the third day after his milah and explains that this repeats at every bris. Hashem comes at the bris itself, holding the mohel's hand as He held Avraham's and signing the bris Himself, and again on the third day to visit and bless.

title.en: Chevron, a share for all, and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach ties Parshas Chayei Sarah's purchase of Chevron and the Me'aras HaMachpela to the place of Avraham's bris, explains that everyone at a bris has a share in it, and closes with blessings for the parents, the family and the child.

catalogTitle: התורה יורדת בסתר המדריגות כדי שכל אחד יוכל לתפוס בה' ועי"ז זוכה ליחוד נפלא ועצום בהקב"ה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter four, that the Torah came down through hidden rungs so that every Jew can grasp it, and that through learning Torah and doing mitzvos a person is bound to Hashem Himself in a union greater than the souls in Gan Eden enjoy.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins with the idea that this world is an imaginary world, while the truth is that Hashem is present here as before creation. Since no thought can grasp Hashem and the Torah is one with Him, Hashem brought the Torah down like water, rung by rung, clothing it in halachos, words and physical mitzvos, as radium is held in a lead case. Thought, speech and even the shaking of a Jew in learning are clothed in Torah, so the whole person becomes a chariot for the Shechinah. We do not feel it because aveiros insulate the body from the soul, yet one should believe it. This is why one hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world is better than all of Olam Haba, where souls only enjoy the rays of the Shechinah. He compares it to embracing a king through his garments, digresses on the seven notes of creation and Shabbos, contrasts philosophers with ovdei Hashem through the Satmar Rav at his Shabbos table, and answers a question about water as chesed.

en: This world is an imaginary world in which Hashem hides Himself, while in truth He is present here just as before creation.
Since no thought can grasp Hashem and the Torah is one with Him, Hashem lowered the Torah through hidden rungs, like water flowing down, into halachos and physical mitzvos.
The Torah changed only its form, not its essence, like water that becomes ice or steam and stays the same water.
When a person learns Torah with thought, speech and action, his whole being is bound to Hashem and becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, even if he does not feel it.
Aveiros insulate the body from the soul, so the body does not feel the Shechinah that the soul knows is resting upon it.
In Olam Haba the souls enjoy only the rays of the Shechinah, while in this world Hashem Himself is present in the Torah and mitzvos, which is why one hour here is better than all of Olam Haba.
Embracing Hashem through the Torah is like embracing a king through his garments: the king himself is in one's arms.

candidateTopics: Torah as the descent of Hashem through hidden rungs
union with Hashem through Torah study
aveiros as insulation between body and soul
the seven voices and musical notes of creation

title.en: This world as an imaginary world

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that Hashem lowered Himself into the Torah and its mitzvos so every soul can understand it, and explains that the physical world we think is real is the imaginary world, while Hashem fills it as before creation.

title.en: Torah descends like water through hidden rungs

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Torah is compared to water that flows down to the lowest place, brings the mashal of radium held in a lead case, and shows how the Torah clothed itself in halachos like those of sukkah, which are all names of Hashem, changing its form but not its essence, like water, ice and steam.

title.en: Thought, speech, action and the shaking of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah reaches down past thought into speech and the physical actions of learning, even the shaking over a Gemara, tells the account of two mixed-up children recognized by their shaking, and explains the shaking with the passuk that the soul of man is a candle of Hashem.

title.en: Bound to Hashem, but insulated by aveiros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one who learns Torah is bound from head to toe to Hashem and becomes a chariot for the Shechinah, as great tzaddikim visibly felt, and that we do not feel it because aveiros insulate the body from the soul; still, he says, one should believe it and act accordingly.

title.en: One hour in this world is better than Olam Haba

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk of the shield of Hashem's will that surrounds the tzaddik and the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos that one hour of teshuvah and good deeds in this world is better than all of Olam Haba, explaining that here Hashem's full presence rests on a person, while in Olam Haba only a light of the Shechinah reaches the souls.

title.en: The pleasure of grasping: Ziv HaShechinah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the rays of the Shechinah to the rays of the sun, describes the pleasure of understanding a sugya or a scientific discovery, and explains that this is the pleasure tzaddikim have in Olam Haba as they rise from level to level, while no creature, not even the angels, can grasp Hashem Himself.

title.en: Embracing the King through His garments

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that understanding a mitzvah through a blatt Gemara is grasping Hashem Himself, unlike the souls in Gan Eden, and answers that the physical clothing does not matter, with the mashal of embracing a king through garments and sleeves; he connects this to the passuk 'His right hand embraces me' and to the Torah given from the right, the attribute of chesed and water.

title.en: The seven voices: music, creation and Shabbos

summary.en: In a digression, the Mashgiach explains that Kabbalas Shabbos begins with Mizmor l'Dovid Havu, whose seven voices are the seven notes of music with which the seven days were created, says this world is wonderful for one who uses it for closeness to Hashem, and describes the harmony of the third, the seventh day as the completion that lets us sing, and Eretz Yisrael and the Kinneres as the seventh of the lands and seas.

title.en: Tanya is for ovdei Hashem, not philosophers

summary.en: Returning to his point, the Mashgiach explains that water is chesed and the source of every pleasure, so Hashem's right hand embraces a person through the Torah. He then says the Ba'al HaTanya wrote for ovdei Hashem: a philosopher may see depth in the Tanya but has no taste for the union with Hashem, like a person with no ear for music.

title.en: The Satmar Rav's Shabbos fish

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how he saw the Satmar Rav at his Friday night tish, his face flaming at Kiddush and eating the fish with delight because he felt the Shabbos in it, and tells of a poor Jew who asked Hashem to give him Shabbos for his challos and fish. He concludes that the Tanya spoke to Chassidim who understood and were delighted by it.

title.en: Why water is chesed: a question

summary.en: A listener asks that other sefarim describe water as passive and static; the Mashgiach answers that this is a mashal, but in its depth water reaches out and spreads, and it goes down to lower places to bring growth to the world, unlike gas, which spreads but rises away.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Toldos, the Mashgiach explains that the parsha in which all three Avos are together gives blessing and strength to three generations together: grandfather, father and child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the parsha is called Toldos, offspring, because it holds the strength, blessing and flow that pass from parents to children. He brings the story of the Yitav Lev, who sat with his grandfather the Yismach Moshe and his father, when the Yismach Moshe asked that all three generations say Torah, in line with the verse that Torah will not depart from a man's mouth, his children's and his grandchildren's. At this bris, too, three generations are together, grandfather, father and the newborn entering the great mitzvah of milah, with Torah and chesed together. Toldos, he says, is the one parsha where all three Avos are together, from Yaakov's birth until Avraham's passing, and this brings blessing to Klal Yisroel and their children. He closes with a blessing for the family.

en: The parsha is named Toldos because it holds the strength and blessing that pass from parents to children.
When three generations are together, Torah is promised to stay with the family, as the Yismach Moshe showed by having all three say Torah.
At this bris three generations, grandfather, father and child, are together in Torah and chesed.
Toldos is the only parsha in which all three Avos are found together, and this brings blessing to Klal Yisroel and their children.

title.en: Three generations and Parshas Toldos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the name Toldos as the blessing passed to children, brings the Yismach Moshe's wish that three generations say Torah together, and ties the three generations at this bris to the one parsha where all three Avos are together, ending with a blessing for the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Parshas Vayetzei, the Mashgiach explains why Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda was not: milah shows that a person can perfect himself, which is the path of teshuvah of Yehuda and Moshiach ben David.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach notes that this week's parsha tells of the births of Yehuda and Yosef, the roots of the two Meshichim. Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda was not, though Moshiach ben David is higher. He answers with the Chinuch: milah shows that man is created incomplete and can perfect himself. There are two paths, the tzaddik who never sinned, Yosef, the 'tzaddik yesod olam', and the baal teshuvah, Yehuda, from whom comes David, who taught teshuvah. So Yehuda was born with an orlah, to perfect himself. He then brings a vort that most fruits lose their status when crushed, while grapes and wheat rise to wine and bread. With this he explains why Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, consoled Avraham with bread and wine: they show that what is crushed can be raised. He closes with blessings that the child carry both qualities.

en: Yosef, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, was born circumcised, while Yehuda, root of the higher Moshiach ben David, was not.
Following the Chinuch, milah shows that a person is created incomplete and can perfect himself.
Yosef represents the tzaddik who never sinned, and Yehuda, through David, represents teshuvah.
Wine and bread show that what is crushed and worked can be raised to a higher level.
Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, could not show Avraham from milah that one can repair oneself, so he brought bread and wine.

candidateTopics: Moshiach ben David and Moshiach ben Yosef

title.en: Why Yosef was born circumcised and Yehuda not

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yosef, root of Moshiach ben Yosef, was born circumcised while Yehuda, root of the higher Moshiach ben David, was not. With the Chinuch's reason for milah he explains that Yosef is the tzaddik who never sinned, while Yehuda and David stand for teshuvah, a person perfecting himself.

title.en: Malki-tzedek's bread and wine, and blessings

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a vort that grapes and wheat, unlike other fruits, are raised when crushed into wine and bread. With it he explains that Malki-tzedek, born circumcised, consoled Avraham with bread and wine to show that one can repair oneself, ties this to the two Meshichim, and blesses the child to carry both their qualities.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Vayetzei, the Mashgiach explains that Levi received his name from Hashem at the Kisei HaKavod at his bris, and that the bris carries the whole Torah, which is why shevet Levi is bound to it.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that the mitzvah of milah comes while the child is still small, and that compared to the height of this mitzvah all are small; it is the root of all of Yiddishkeit. From the week's parsha he brings the passuk of Levi's naming and the teaching of Chazal that the angels brought Levi up to the Kisei HaKavod (Throne of Glory) and Hashem Himself named him. He asks when this happened and answers: at his bris, when a name is given. At a bris Hashem is present openly, as with Avraham Avinu's bris and 'Vayera elav Hashem'. Bris equals 612 and with milah 613, so the whole Torah comes to a bris. Shevet Levi kept milah in Mitzrayim, which is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim. He closes with brachos for the child named Moshe, from a family of talmidei chachamim.

en: The Mashgiach says that compared to the height of the mitzvah of milah everyone is small, and that it is the root of all of Yiddishkeit.
According to Chazal the angels brought Levi up to the Kisei HaKavod and Hashem named him, and the Mashgiach explains that this was at his bris, where a name is given.
At a bris Hashem is revealed openly, as at Avraham Avinu's bris, where the Torah says 'Vayera elav Hashem'.
The word bris equals 612, and with the mitzvah of milah itself 613, so the bris includes all the mitzvos and the whole Torah comes to it.
Shevet Levi alone kept milah in Mitzrayim, so they are bound to the bris, and that is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim.

candidateTopics: naming a child at the bris

title.en: Levi named at the Kisei HaKavod at his bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the height of the mitzvah of milah and brings from the parsha that Hashem named Levi at the Kisei HaKavod, explaining that this happened at his bris. He then shows that Hashem is revealed at a bris, as at Avraham Avinu's, and that bris (612) with milah makes 613, so the whole Torah comes to a bris.

title.en: Shevet Levi, the bris, and brachos for Moshe

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that shevet Levi kept milah in Mitzrayim, which is why the bentching at a bris is said with the permission of the kohanim and leviim, and ties Levi to Moshe Rabbeinu and to the child's name Moshe. He closes with brachos for the child, from a family of talmidei chachamim on both sides, and for the parents and grandparents.

catalogTitle: ע"י לימוד תורה - כביכול תופס ה' בתוכו' וה' מתיחד בו ביחוד עצום ונפלא.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter five: when a Jew truly understands Torah he and the Torah envelop each other, and since Hashem encased Himself in the Torah, this is a union with Hashem that no mitzvah and no angel reaches.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach first reviews a passage of the Ba'al HaTanya about ten Jews: the Shechinah rests on any ten, so a group that sits idle 'squeezes' the Shechinah, and he brings the Maggid of Mezritch's saying that an angel would be burnt up among ten Jews. The Ba'al HaTanya therefore urges simple people to learn the aggados of Ein Yaakov, where the deepest secrets of the Torah are hidden. Turning to chapter five, the Mashgiach explains that a mitzvah envelops a person only from outside, while Torah understood with the mind is a double union: the person grasps the subject and the subject envelops him. Though no thought can grasp Hashem, He encased Himself in the halachos like radioactive matter in lead, so a Jew who understands a halacha grasps Hashem's will. Therefore Torah is called food and mitzvos clothing. He ends with sukkah as surrounding light and the Torah of Simchas Torah as inner light.

en: Wherever ten Jews gather the Shechinah rests on them, so idle talk there presses on the Shechinah; the Mashgiach says ten Jews together should learn Torah.
Many aggados of the Gemara that seem senseless hide the highest secrets of the Torah, which is why the Ba'al HaTanya tells simple people to learn Ein Yaakov.
A mitzvah envelops a person from outside, but Torah that is understood is a double union: the person envelops the Torah and the Torah envelops him.
No thought, not even of angels, can grasp Hashem, yet a Jew grasps Him in Torah, because Hashem and the Torah are one and He encased Himself in the halachos.
The mitzvah of knowing Torah with the mind surpasses even the mitzvah of speaking words of Torah, because the Torah enters within the person.
Torah is therefore called food, which becomes part of the body, while the mitzvos are called clothing.

candidateTopics: Torah study as union with Hashem
Torah as food, mitzvos as clothing

title.en: The Shechinah among ten Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Ba'al HaTanya's words that the Shechinah rests wherever ten Jews gather, and brings the Maggid of Mezritch's saying that an angel would be burnt up among them. When they sit idle, he explains, they squeeze the Shechinah, which is one cause of the length of the golus.

title.en: The hidden secrets in the aggados

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Ba'al HaTanya tells the common people to learn Ein Yaakov: aggados that sound like nonsense, such as the bird whose egg destroyed sixty cities, wrap the highest secrets of the Torah. Answering a listener who asks whether this is dangerous, he says that the straight walk in the Torah's ways while the crooked stumble.

title.en: Perek five: Torah envelops from both sides

summary.en: Opening chapter five, the Mashgiach notes that the Tanya develops one theme step by step. A mitzvah envelops a person like a cloak, but Torah is more: one who is immersed in learning grasps the Torah within him while it surrounds him from without, a double union.

title.en: Grasping Hashem encased in Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that although no thought, not even an angel's, grasps Hashem, a Jew who learns does, because Hashem and the Torah are one. He compares it to radioactive matter held safely in a lead box and to a caress through a sleeve, and reads the Tanya's words on the mind enveloping the subject it understands.

title.en: A halachah is Hashem's will

summary.en: Unlike a mathematical equation, a halachah is Hashem's wisdom and will, even in cases that may never happen, such as the Gemara's question about one born with two heads. Understanding it is a wondrous two-way union that has no parallel in the physical world.

title.en: Knowing Torah surpasses every mitzvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the mitzvah of knowing Torah is above all mitzvos, even above speaking words of Torah, since in lulav or tefillin the holiness only surrounds the person. He brings the Ba'al HaTanya's ruling about thinking Torah before the blessing, and shows with a boy learning 'tashma' that each person must work to his own full capacity.

title.en: Torah is food, mitzvos are clothing

summary.en: Torah that is learned becomes a person's food and the mitzvos he does become his clothing, which the Mashgiach says is why clothing costs more than food: money should be spent on mitzvos, while Torah is given free. Like bread absorbed into the body, understood Torah becomes part of a person, and spoken Torah is both garment and food.

title.en: Sukkah surrounds, Torah is within

summary.en: After a question about kavanah in mitzvos, the Mashgiach explains that the sukkah is a surrounding light and that on Simchas Torah the inner light of the Torah follows. He connects this to the generation of the flood, which merited only the ark, a kind of sukkah, and to Shavuos and Shemini Atzeres, which have no special mitzvah.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chevron and Shechem, two of the three places in Eretz Yisroel bought with money, are the places of mitzvas milah, and that the bris had to be acquired with mesiras nefesh, which is why the seudah of a bris is so great a simcha.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Midrash that although Hashem gave all of Eretz Yisroel to the Avos, three places were bought with money: Har HaMoriah, the Me'aras HaMachpelah and Shechem. Building on the idea that the whole land is a Sefer Torah, with a halacha written into every piece of it, he explains that Chevron is the place of milah: this is why Mamre, its owner, merited that Hashem revealed Himself in his portion, and why the Machpelah was shown to Avraham on the third day of his milah. Shechem, the burial place of Yosef, is also a place of milah, and its people were the great orlah that had to be removed; all three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, can be seen there. Yosef drew strength from Chevron and Shechem before going into exile. Because the bris is the root of everything, it could not come as a gift: it had to cost money and blood, and the joy of the seudah is the joy of mesiras nefesh.

en: Three places in Eretz Yisroel were bought with money even though the whole land was given to the Avos: Har HaMoriah, the Me'aras HaMachpelah and Shechem.
Every part of Eretz Yisroel has a halacha written into it, and Chevron is the place of mitzvas milah.
The Me'aras HaMachpelah can belong only to one connected to milah, so it was revealed to Avraham in the merit of the simcha of his milah.
Shechem, the place of Yosef, is also a place of milah, and all three parts of milah, milah, periah and metzitzah, are seen there.
The bris could not be acquired as a gift; it had to cost money and blood, through mesiras nefesh.
The great simcha of the seudah of a bris is the joy of having given blood for Hashem, and each Jew there accepts to do every mitzvah with mesiras nefesh.

candidateTopics: Eretz Yisroel as a Sefer Torah

title.en: Three places bought; Chevron, the place of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that three places were bought with money, and the Gemara that Osniel ben Kenaz restored the forgotten halachos after conquering Kiryat Sefer, explained as owning the land where they were written. From this he explains Rashi that Mamre merited Hashem's revelation in his portion because he owned Chevron, the place of milah.

title.en: The Machpelah revealed in the merit of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham was shown the Me'aras HaMachpelah on the third day of his milah, long before Sarah died, and answers that it is the place of milah and belongs only to one connected to milah. He adds the Gemara on Pinchas that a tzaddik is buried in the place of his root, and asks how Shechem, Yosef's burial place, fits.

title.en: Shechem, Yosef and the orlah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Sfas Emes that the holiest place holds the greatest orlah, so Shechem, a place of milah, was held by Shechem ben Chamor the Chivi, who could not truly be circumcised. He shows that Yosef's root is in Shechem through Osnas, and that Yosef had to pass through Chevron and Shechem to gain the strength of milah before going down to Mitzrayim.

title.en: Milah, periah and metzitzah in Shechem

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that metzitzah, though by the plain Gemara a matter of danger, is in the inner meaning part of milah: drawing out the bad even from far and deep places. All three parts of milah appear in Shechem: the people were circumcised, the converts were turned to holiness, and the surrounding nations came to war and were defeated.

title.en: Why the places of milah had to be bought

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that because Chevron and Shechem are the places of milah, the greatest kelipos in Eretz Yisroel are found there before the coming of Moshiach. He explains that although the whole land was a gift to Avraham, Har HaMoriah, Chevron and Shechem needed a strong kinyan with money, because one cannot be sure of these things through a gift alone; they require mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The joy of the bris seudah: mesiras nefesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the seudah of a bris is a greater simcha than other mitzvos, and answers that Avraham acquired the kedushah of the bris with his blood and mesiras nefesh, so the bris had to cost money and blood. He brings a saying of Rebbe Avraham Mordechai of Ger that nothing is reached without mesiras nefesh, and closes with brachos for the child and for the geulah.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on 19 Kislev, the Mashgiach explains that the power of Yishmael rests on his empty milah, and that a Jewish bris done with joy, in the days leading to Chanukah, helps break that power and bring the geulah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by comparing the week of Chanukah to the week of Tisha b'Av, which has laws of lessening joy. Today, 19 Kislev, is the hilula of the Maggid and the release of the Ba'al haTanya, and She'elos uTeshuvos min haShamayim calls it a day of good tidings. He ties this to the day's news: every nation has a heavenly prince, kings below fall only when their prince falls, and a prince of Yishmael has now fallen. Yishmael's twelve nesi'im are twelve angels, and Chanukah, with its reading of the Nesi'im, breaks them; once the fall begins it continues. Yishmael's whole power is his milah, which according to the Zera Kodesh is an empty milah, so his claim to Eretz Yisroel is empty too. A Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy breaks that power. He closes with Moshe, Eliyahu and Moshiach, the child's name Moshe Eliyahu, and brachos.

en: The Mashgiach argues that just as the week of Tisha b'Av has laws of lessening joy, the week of Chanukah, which begins on 19 Kislev, surely carries joy.
Kings below do not fall unless their prince above falls; the day's news shows that a prince of Yishmael in heaven has fallen.
Chanukah, when the parsha of the Nesi'im is read, breaks the power of Yishmael's twelve nesi'im, and once one falls the others will follow.
The whole power of Yishmael is his milah, and a Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy breaks that power.
The Mashgiach says that today's bris and its preparation, from the shalom zachar on, contributed to the fall of the prince of Yishmael, and in its merit Jews will be helped.
Moshiach is the joining of the souls of Moshe and David, together with Eliyahu, and a child named Moshe Eliyahu is tied to the geulah.

title.en: 19 Kislev, a day of good tidings

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the week of Chanukah to the week of Tisha b'Av and notes that 19 Kislev is the hilula of the Maggid and the release of the Ba'al haTanya, called a day of good tidings in She'elos uTeshuvos min haShamayim. He turns to the day's news and explains that every nation has a prince above, and kings below fall only when he falls.

title.en: Chanukah and the twelve nesi'im of Yishmael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yishmael's twelve nesi'im are twelve angels, and brings the Midrash and Targum Yonasan in Parshas Naso that the offerings of the Chanukas haMizbe'ach break them; this is why the Nesi'im are read on Chanukah. Once the fall of the sitra achra begins it continues, and today a prince of Yishmael has fallen.

title.en: Yishmael's empty milah, the bris and Moshiach

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yishmael's whole power is his milah, which according to the Zera Kodesh is empty, so his claim to Eretz Yisroel is empty too; a Jewish bris done with love, fear and joy, with its preparation, helps break that power. He then brings the Chasam Sofer on Moshe, David and Eliyahu in Moshiach, ties it to the Harachaman prayers and the child's name, Moshe Eliyahu, and closes with brachos.

catalogTitle: כנגד עשר ספירות דקדושה יש זה לעומת זה “עשר כתרין דמסאבותא” . סימן להשראת הקדושה - שבטל להקב"ה ובטומאה להיפוך.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter six, the Mashgiach explains that opposite the ten holy powers of the soul stand ten 'crowns of impurity', and that holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem, which every Jew is in potential.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter six: just as the soul of holiness has ten powers, the soul from kelipas nogah has ten powers of impurity, 'zeh l'umas zeh'. He notes that only impurity is called 'crowns', because it attributes greatness to itself, and links its ten to the ten sons of Haman. Impurity, he adds, is never truly ten but nine or eleven, shown by the Teivah's eleven amos, the Mishkan's eleven goat-hair curtains and the eleven spices of the ketores. He then explains that the middos can serve Hashem or nonsense; there is no neutral reshus, and pointless pursuits are 're'us ruach', a breaking of the soul's connection. Holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem; every Jew is batel in potential, as the history of mesiras nefesh shows, an inheritance from Avraham Avinu. He closes with a story of the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter and questions from listeners.

en: Opposite the ten holy powers of the soul there are ten powers of impurity from kelipas nogah, so a person can become a seat either for holiness or for impurity.
The powers of impurity are called 'crowns' because impurity has a sense of self and attributes greatness to itself.
The ten of impurity are not truly ten but nine or eleven; the number ten is reserved for holiness.
There is no neutral reshus: whatever is not done for the sake of Hashem belongs to the other side, the sitra achra.
Holiness rests only on what is batel to Hashem, and every Jew is batel to Hashem at least in potential.
The readiness of Jews to give their lives for Hashem is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu.

candidateTopics: kelipas nogah and the animal soul
nine and eleven in the realm of impurity
ketores and nullifying the sitra achra

title.en: Ten powers of holiness and ten of impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the ten holy powers of the soul and introduces Tanya chapter six: opposite them, 'zeh l'umas zeh', stand ten powers of impurity in the soul from kelipas nogah, so a person can become a seat for either side.

title.en: Why impurity is called 'crowns'

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that the word 'crowns' appears only for impurity, because impurity is haughty and sees itself as something. He lists the seven bad middos from the four elements and the intellect above them, and links the ten crowns to the ten sons of Haman in the Megillah.

title.en: Impurity is nine or eleven, never ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ten of impurity only appear to be ten and are really nine or eleven. He shows this from Rashi's eleven amos of the Teivah, the eleven goat-hair curtains of the Mishkan, the eleven spices of the ketores and the order in which they are listed, and the eleven verses said on Motzaei Shabbos.

title.en: Middos for Hashem or for nonsense

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the same middos can serve Hashem, such as chesed, gevurah for milchemes Hashem and pride in being a Jew, or can be spent on nonsense, like insisting on a designer tie or anger over trifles. There is no reshus: it is either a mitzvah or an aveirah, and the middos follow the level of a person's intellect, as with a child.

title.en: Re'us ruach: breaking the connection

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that worldly pursuits that are not for Hashem are 'havel' and 're'us ruach'. He illustrates with a ball game, where grown men scream over a stitched pigskin, and explains re'us as breaking: such pursuits sever the soul's connection to Hashem like a cut wire.

title.en: The ice cream: two sides of the fence

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains 'sitra achra' as the other side of the fence. Ice cream eaten to lift one's spirits is a mitzvah, and recreation in measure for health is good, but indulgence for its own sake falls to the other side, since there is no reshus.

title.en: Holiness rests on what is batel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem's holiness rests only on what is batel to Him: the angels in fact, like a machine run by its operator, and every Jew at least in potential, as shown by Jews throughout history who gave their lives rather than commit avodah zarah.

title.en: Chalav akum and readiness for mesiras nefesh

summary.en: Citing the Tzemach Tzedek on Jews who are not ready for mesiras nefesh, the Mashgiach digresses to chalav akum: government-inspected milk, the views of Rav Moshe Feinstein and the Chazon Ish, and a story of a Rebbe who made himself vomit milk he learned was chalav akum. He returns to say such things can dull a person's readiness to give his life.

title.en: Avraham's inheritance and Fayvish the thief

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that readiness for mesiras nefesh is an inheritance from Avraham Avinu, and that the Ba'al HaTanya says a Jew who sins remains holy because he is ready to die for Hashem. He tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov's daughter Adel, who said Hashem chose wisely, since even a thief named Fayvish gave his life rather than convert, and adds that at the shofar of Moshiach even the farthest Jew will run after him.

title.en: Questions: intention and Krias Shema

summary.en: Answering a listener, the Mashgiach suggests that an act begun for Hashem keeps its first intention even if the mind wanders, as with learning Gemara, and that the morning declaration of readiness for mesiras nefesh carries through the day. On whether to imagine actual death at Krias Shema, he says the sefarim say to imagine it.

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the last day of Chanukah, the Mashgiach blesses the child with the words 'Elokim yechonecha beni', as Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once blessed a child born on Chanukah, that he be a Chanukah child.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach says he only wants to give a brachah. He relates that Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once said to a child born on Chanukah 'Elokim yechonecha beni' (may G-d be gracious to you, my son), wishing that he be a Chanukah child, since the seforim say this passuk alludes to Chanukah. The child at this bris was born on the first day of Chanukah and his bris falls on the last day, so the Mashgiach gives him the same blessing: to be a Chanukah child, a child of dveikus and avodas Hashem, bringing nachas to his parents, to the Ribono shel Olam and to all Jews.

en: Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz once blessed a child born on Chanukah with 'Elokim yechonecha beni', wishing that he be a Chanukah child.
The Mashgiach notes that the seforim say the passuk 'Elokim yechonecha beni' alludes to Chanukah.
Since this child was born on the first day of Chanukah and his bris is on the last day, the Mashgiach gives him the same blessing.
He blesses the child with dveikus and avodas Hashem, and that he bring nachas to his parents, to the Ribono shel Olam and to all Jews.

title.en: A brachah for a Chanukah child

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates how Rebbe Chaim Meir of Vizhnitz blessed a child born on Chanukah with 'Elokim yechonecha beni', and gives the same blessing to this child, born on the first day of Chanukah with his bris on the last, together with wishes for dveikus, avodas Hashem and nachas.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Erev Shabbos Chanukah

oneLiner.en: At a bris on erev Shabbos Chanukah, the Mashgiach connects the bris, Chanukah, Shabbos and the child's name Elisha to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy, healing and long life, and blesses the family.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by noting that it is erev Shabbos Chanukah, so he will speak briefly. At a bris the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are revealed, and on Chanukah as well, so a bris on Chanukah is a double good. Since it falls on the third day of Chanukah, he links it to one of the attributes of mercy. Shabbos, which is being prepared for, is tied to 'erech', from which come healing and long life. He blesses the child, parents, grandparents and all who take part with the blessing of Eliyahu Hanavi, present at every bris. The child is named Elisha; someone pointed out that Elisha brought healing even to a non-Jew, Naaman, so all the more for Jews. This week's sedra contains a kal vachomer, as Rashi notes, and he cites tzaddikim that the thirteen attributes of mercy parallel the thirteen rules of Torah exegesis, kal vachomer corresponding to 'Keil', chessed. The sandek too stands for chessed. He closes with blessings.

en: At a bris the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy are revealed, and also on Chanukah, so a bris on Chanukah is doubly great.
Shabbos is connected to 'erech', the source of healing and long life.
Elisha brought healing even to Naaman, a non-Jew; all the more so will the name bring healing to Jews.
The thirteen attributes of mercy parallel the thirteen rules of Torah exegesis, and kal vachomer corresponds to 'Keil', the attribute of chessed.
The sandek also represents chessed.

title.en: A bris on Chanukah: mercy, healing and the name Elisha

summary.en: The Mashgiach links the bris, the third day of Chanukah and Shabbos to the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy and to healing, draws a kal vachomer from Elisha healing Naaman, ties kal vachomer to the attribute of chessed, and blesses the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris in the week of Vayechi, the Mashgiach explains that Yosef served as sandek for the children of Machir ben Menashe and so turned Gilead, a place of the mazal of bloodshed, into the source of Eliyahu, the angel of the bris.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the passuk that the children of Machir ben Menashe were born on Yosef's knees, which many explain to mean that Yosef was their sandek. This is said of no other descendants of Yosef. He brings the Gemara that one born under the mazal of Maadim will be a shedder of blood, such as a mohel. Machir's son was Gilead, and the Gemara says Gilead was a place where murderers were common, a place of Maadim. Yosef, with the holiness of the bris, gave Gilead a tikun so that from there would come Eliyahu HaGiladi, the angel of the bris: the blood of Gilead became the blood of milah. He connects Vayechi, the sedra of Yosef, to bris milah, and ends with blessings that the child grow up a tzaddik and chacham and bring nachas to his parents and grandparents.

en: The children of Machir ben Menashe being born on Yosef's knees is understood to mean that Yosef was their sandek, something said of no other offspring of Yosef.
The Gemara says one born under Maadim will shed blood, and one of the possibilities is a mohel.
Gilead, Machir's son and the region of that name, is a place of Maadim, where murderers were common.
Through serving as sandek, Yosef drew the holiness of milah into Gilead so that Eliyahu HaGiladi, the angel of the bris, would come from there.

title.en: Yosef as sandek and Eliyahu of Gilead

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the passuk about Machir's children born on Yosef's knees as Yosef being sandek, brings the Gemara on the mazal of Maadim and on Gilead, explains that Yosef made Gilead the source of Eliyahu, angel of the bris, ties Vayechi to milah, and blesses the family.

catalogTitle: הטומאה הוא כקוף בפני אדם. החילוק בין קדושה וטומאה - ביטול להקב"ה. יניקת הקליפה מבחינת אחוריים' שלש קליפות הטמאות וקליפת נוגה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 6, the Mashgiach explains that tumah imitates kedusha like a monkey imitates a man, that the whole difference is bittul to Hashem, and that the klipos live only from a tiny spark drawn from the 'back side' of holiness.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that tumah mimics kedusha: the kuf imitates the hei as a monkey imitates a man, and Achashverosh's feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash. The difference is bittul: kedusha is nullified to Hashem, while tumah stands as an independent entity. He shows how Torah learned with yiras Shamayim and every gathering of ten Yidden draw the Shechinah, even the ten spies. A separate entity lives only from a tiny spark of kedusha given 'from behind', renewed every moment, and that spark is in exile; the Yid's task is to free it, and Chanukah and Purim bring kedusha down to the lowest places. He then distinguishes the three impure klipos, which cannot be elevated now, from what is nourished through them, explains the four klipos and the chayos of Yechezkel's Merkava, and closes with male and female in kedusha and in the sitra achra, the seven nations as middos, and why the inanimate is not listed.

en: Tumah has ten sefiros like kedusha and imitates it, like a monkey imitating a man, but it is not batel to Hashem.
Torah learned with yiras Shamayim makes a person batel and brings the Shechinah, while ten Yidden together always have the Shechinah with them.
A separate entity gets its existence through countless contractions, from the 'back side' of kedusha, and this is renewed at every moment.
The spark of kedusha that gives life to tumah is in exile, and the task of a Yid is to extract and redeem such sparks.
What draws its life from the three impure klipos cannot be elevated in this world, until Moshiach comes.
In kedusha the male, chesed, rules over the female, din, while in the sitra achra the female is stronger.

three impure klipos and klipas nogah

title.en: Tumah imitates kedusha like a monkey

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that tumah mimics kedusha: the kuf imitates the hei of Hashem's Name, and Achashverosh's feast imitated the Beis HaMikdash. The difference is that kedusha is batel to Hashem while tumah stands on its own, cut off from its supply; yet every Yid is inwardly batel.

title.en: Torah with yiras Shamayim and the ten

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why the Shechinah rests on one who learns Torah, provided he learns with yiras Shamayim, comparing Torah without it to an empty capsule or an unplugged radio. He then shows that ten Yidden always have the Shechinah, and that even the ten spies, from whom davar shebikdusha is learned, had it because inwardly they were tzaddikim.

title.en: Life from the back side, renewed each moment

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that whatever is not batel is a separate entity, yet it exists only through Hashem's word, contracted countless times into a tiny spark given from the 'back side'. He stresses that creation is not a historical fact but happens anew every moment.

title.en: The spark in exile and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tanya's chiddush that even the energy of a rasha doing an aveirah is created at that moment from Hashem, a tiny spark that is in exile. He connects this to Chanukah, when the Shechinah comes below ten tefachim, and says the avodah of a Yid is to redeem such sparks.

title.en: A world mostly evil; Shabbos and Chanukah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that this world is the world of klipos, mostly evil, as seen in nature. On Shabbos and Yom Tov a Yid rises above it, since melachah is a curse; on Chanukah and Purim, days when work is permitted, kedusha comes down to him. He ties this to Eliezer leaving the curse for blessing and to Shabbos Mevarchim Kislev.

title.en: Three impure klipos and the Merkava

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the lower level of klipos, the three impure klipos, cannot be elevated until Moshiach. He brings the four klipos Yechezkel passed on the way to the Merkava, explains why the Ba'al HaTanya does not spell them all out, and shows from the lion and eagle of the Merkava how gevurah becomes impure on its way down. An audience question on mentioning resha'im follows.

title.en: What draws life from the impure klipos

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the levels of creation, domem, tzome'ach, chai and medaber, and explains that the existence of non-kosher animals and of forbidden growths like orlah and kilai hakerem comes from the three impure klipos, which is why they are forbidden from their inception. He notes that the Tanya does not list domem and begins to explain why.

title.en: Chesed over din: male and female

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in kedusha the male, chesed, is meant to dominate the female, din, and digresses to criticize the modern equality movement, contrasting it with the harmony of Jewish homes. He connects this to Esav's wives going first and to giving the right side precedence over the left.

title.en: The Or HaChaim's dream and the seven nations

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Or HaChaim's dream of a male and a female dog, showing that in the sitra achra the female is stronger. He maps the seven nations onto the middos, explains that the Girgashi is malchus and left voluntarily, which is why domem is batel and not listed, and sums up the perek: ten crowns of tumah exist mainly in this world, while kedusha is batel to Hashem.

catalogTitle: ברית מילה: Bris Milah - Vaera Shovevim

oneLiner.en: At a bris on the Friday of Shovevim in the week of Vaera, the Mashgiach explains that at a bris Hashem shows Himself, as He did to the Avos with the name Keil Shakai, and ties the bris to refuah, the leshonos of geulah and the child's name Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach cites the Ba'al HaTanya that 'Va'eira' in the passuk means 'I appeared', and adds another reading: Hashem shows Himself also to the children, not only to the Avos, at certain times of favor, to one who wants to feel it. At the bris Avraham was told 'I am Keil Shakai', the name of the bris, and the passuk says Hashem appeared to the Avos with that name; so at every bris, even today, Hashem shows Himself. The bris falls on a Friday of Shovevim in Vaera, where the tikun of Shovevim begins. The Zera Kodesh says the plagues were healing for Israel, and the Gemara says refuah is the eighth bracha because milah is on the eighth day. The child is named Yisrael, a name that holds all of Klal Yisrael, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov was named Yisrael. He closes with the blessing of Torah, chuppah and good deeds, and wishes for the geulah.

en: Beyond 'I appeared', 'Va'eira' also means that Hashem shows Himself to the children, not only the Avos, at times of favor, to one who wants to feel it.
Keil Shakai is the name of the bris, so at every bris, even in later generations, Hashem shows Himself.
Refuah is the eighth bracha because milah is on the eighth day, and the plagues of Vaera were healing for Israel.
The name Yisrael includes all of Klal Yisrael, which is why the Ba'al Shem Tov carried that name.

title.en: Va'eira: Hashem appears at every bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Va'eira' as Hashem showing Himself to the children through the name Keil Shakai of the bris, links the bris on a Friday of Shovevim to refuah and the geulah, explains the child's name Yisrael, and blesses the family.

oneLiner.en: At a bris during Shovevim, the Mashgiach explains that milah both draws chassadim onto Klal Yisroel and brings judgment on the nations, and that a bris on a Friday of Shovevim is an especially great tikkun.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a passuk whose first letters and last letters both spell milah, which is rarely found. First letters, he explains, stand for chessed, drawing good onto Klal Yisroel, and last letters for din on the wicked. He shows the same pair in the Exodus, where the plagues struck Mitzrayim and healed the Jews, and in the Megillah: the first letters of Esther's words 'yavo hamelech veHaman hayom' draw chassadim onto Klal Yisroel, while the last letters of Haman's words draw din onto the nations. Milah has both sides: removing the orlah, and drawing chassadim from Avraham Avinu, which is why it was given as the Jews went into exile. In Shovevim, the time of tikkun, a bris is a great tikkun, since Eliyahu Hanavi is present; on Friday, the main day of Shovevim, all the more. He applies this to the dangers facing Jews today and closes with brachos for the child and family.

en: First letters (rashei teivos) stand for the attribute of chessed toward Klal Yisroel, and last letters (sofei teivos) for the attribute of din on the wicked.
In the Megillah, Esther's words carry Hashem's name in their first letters, drawing chassadim on Klal Yisroel, while Haman's words carry it in their last letters, drawing din on the nations.
Milah contains both aspects: it removes the orlah, and it draws chassadim from Avraham Avinu, the head of chessed, onto the Jews.
Shovevim is a time of tikkun, and a bris is a great tikkun, since Eliyahu Hanavi is present at it.
Friday, the sixth day, is the main day of tikkun in Shovevim, so a bris on a Friday of Shovevim is all the more precious.

candidateTopics: exile and protection from the nations

title.en: Milah in first and last letters

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that first letters stand for chessed and last letters for din, shows both in the Exodus and the Megillah, and explains that milah removes the orlah and draws chassadim. He then explains why a bris in Shovevim, and especially on a Friday, is a great tikkun.

title.en: Today's need and brachos for the family

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that Jews today, threatened by the nations and surrounded in Eretz Yisroel, need both sides of milah, and that this bris on a Friday of Shovevim, in a family of Torah, avodah and chessed, draws great chassadim. He blesses the parents and grandparents and recalls the man the child is named after.

catalogTitle: ביאור קליפת נוגה - “קדושים תהיו” - כנגד פריעה. (ישמעאל ומצוות מילה)

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains klipas nogah, the middle layer that a Jew can elevate by using permitted things l'shem shamayim, and shows the same pattern in milah and priyah, which he connects to Yishmael's claim on Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the three wholly impure klipos, which can never be elevated, with klipas nogah, a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on intent. Kosher food is nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten in excess it sinks. Citing the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' and a psychologist's view that enjoyment is a real human need, he sets two conditions: no excess, and l'shem shamayim. Reading Tanya chapter seven, he explains that nogah is all good above but mixed below, and that meat and wine taken for an expanded mind for Torah, or for oneg Shabbos, are elevated. He finds the same rule in milah, where three layers are cut off and the fourth, priyah, is pulled up. This leads to Yishmael's 'empty' milah, Chevron as the place of milah, Shechem as the place of priyah, and the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are not obligated in priyah.

en: The three impure klipos can never be elevated, while klipas nogah is like a scale that tips toward kedushah or tumah depending on how it is used.
Kosher food eaten l'shem shamayim rises like a korban; eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it.
Enjoyment is a real human need, but it must not be in excess and must be for the sake of serving Hashem.
Nogah is entirely good above but mixed with bad in this world; using it for good separates the good and raises it.
In milah the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, and priyah, the fourth layer pulled upward, corresponds to klipas nogah.
Bnei Yishmael, whose body stems from the three impure klipos, can repair only through milah and have no share in priyah, which corresponds to nogah.

title.en: Two extremes and the middle of klipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reviews the previous chapters: through mitzvos a person becomes a seat for kedushah, through aveiros a seat for the three wholly impure klipos. He introduces klipas nogah as a middle layer, like a scale that can tip either way, unlike forbidden food, which can never be elevated.

title.en: Kosher food tips up or down; the Ramban on kedoshim tihyu

summary.en: Kosher food, bound up with the body, is klipas nogah: eaten l'shem shamayim it rises like a korban, eaten without need it is drawn into tumah until teshuvah lifts it again, while the harm of forbidden food stays even after teshuvah. He brings the Ramban on 'kedoshim tihyu' that even permitted pleasures must be sanctified, or a person becomes a degenerate with the Torah's license.

title.en: Why a person needs enjoyment, and its limits

summary.en: The Mashgiach relates a psychologist's point that a person fed without tasting would break down, so enjoyment is a real need; but it must not be in excess and must be l'shem shamayim. A cookie to perk up one's learning is fine, a cookie because of a pleasant aroma is excess, and he cites his rebbe Rav Mendlowitz on a Midrash about the Leviasan's belly being in America.

title.en: Tanya ch. 7: the vital soul and permitted things

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of chapter seven: the vital soul of a Jew, the life of kosher animals, birds and fish, permitted produce, and permitted deeds and words draw from klipas nogah, not from the three impure klipos. He illustrates with someone talking about a ball game, which is no aveirah, and explains that nogah in its source above, the brightness around Hashem in Yechezkel, is entirely good.

title.en: Elevating nogah: meat, wine and oneg Shabbos

summary.en: In this world nogah is a mixture of good and bad on the borderline between the impure klipos and kedushah; used for good, the good separates and rises. He brings the example of fat meat and fragrant wine taken to gain an expanded mind for Torah, citing Rava, and distinguishes this preparation for a mitzvah from oneg Shabbos and Yom Tov, which is a mitzvah in itself.

title.en: Milah and priyah; Yishmael's empty milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same rule in milah: the three layers cut off correspond to the three impure klipos, while the thin fourth layer of priyah is pulled up and elevated, like klipas nogah, and similarly the fourth year of a newly planted tree. He turns to Bnei Yishmael, circumcised at thirteen, and the Zohar that Eretz Yisrael was given to them for their empty milah and stays barren in their hands; the Gemara calls its renewed fruitfulness the clearest sign of the geulah.

title.en: Every place in Eretz Yisrael is a halachah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Temurah about the halachos forgotten after Moshe Rabbeinu's passing, which Osniel ben Kenaz restored through his pilpul, and an explanation that every place in Eretz Yisrael corresponds to a part of the Torah. Kiryas Sefer held those halachos, so mastering them let Osniel conquer the place; the plain meaning and the drash are both true.

title.en: Chevron, the place of milah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Chevron is the territory of the mitzvah of milah, Avraham Avinu's own mitzvah, which is why he bought the Me'aras HaMachpelah with money. The Arabs, who claim Eretz Yisrael through their milah, fight hardest over Chevron, but he says Hashem will shake them out of the land like a sheet, since their milah is only an imitation.

title.en: The imitation and the genuine son of Avraham

summary.en: Responding to a listener, the Mashgiach brings the Ba'al HaTurim on the passage of Yishmael's end followed by the offspring of Yitzchak ben Avraham: Yishmael claims to be the son of Avraham, while Yitzchak is the genuine one. He says each generation has a rasha who embodies Yishmael's accusation, in his time Arafat, whose name he shows equals 'Yishmael ben Avraham' in gematria.

title.en: Shaagas Aryeh: milah without priyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Shaagas Aryeh's chiddush that Bnei Yishmael are obligated only in milah, not priyah, and confirms it from Kabbalah: their body stems from the three impure klipos, so they cannot repair nogah. He adds a gematria on 'tachlis', a Midrash he heard from Rav Mendlowitz, and the halachah that a gentile may bring only an olah, not a shelamim, since only a Jew can make eating into avodah.

title.en: Shechem, the place of priyah, and the closing

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that priyah was given in Yehoshua's time, and Yehoshua comes from Yosef, whose purchased portion is Shechem, so Shechem is the place of priyah as Chevron is the place of milah. He closes that the work of klipas nogah is harnessing bodily pleasure to Hashem's will, like fourth-year fruit, and ends with a story of a seminary professor who spent his whole hour on the root of one word.
